Emotion classification

 is the means by which one may distinguish or contrast one 

emotion

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion

 from another. It is a contested issue in emotion research and in 

affective science

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affective_science

.

Emotions as discrete categories

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=1

]

In 

discrete emotion theory

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_emotion_theory

, all humans are thought to have an innate set of basic emotions that are cross-culturally recognizable. These basic emotions are described as "discrete" because they are believed to be distinguishable by an individual's facial expression and biological processes. 

[1]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-1

 Theorists have conducted studies to determine which emotions are basic. A popular example is 

Paul Ekman

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Ekman

 and his colleagues' cross-cultural study of 1992, in which they concluded that the six basic emotions are 

anger

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anger

, 

disgust

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disgust

, 

fear

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear

, 

happiness

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happiness

, 

sadness

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadness

, and 

surprise

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surprise_(emotion)

. 

[2]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-2

 Ekman explains that there are particular characteristics attached to each of these emotions, allowing them to be expressed in varying degrees in a non-verbal manner. 

[3]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-3

 

[4]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-4

 Each emotion acts as a discrete category rather than an individual emotional state. 

[5]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-ekman-5

Simplicity debate

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=2

]

Humans' subjective experience is that emotions are clearly recognizable in ourselves and others. This apparent ease of recognition has led to the identification of a number of emotions that are said to be basic, and universal among all people. However, a debate among experts has questioned this understanding of what emotions are. There has been recent discussion of the progression on the different views of emotion over the years. 

[6]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-6

On "basic emotion" accounts, activation of an emotion, such as anger, sadness, or fear, is "triggered" by the brain's appraisal of a stimulus or event with respect to the perceiver's goals or survival. In particular, the function, expression, and meaning of different emotions are hypothesized to be biologically distinct from one another. A theme common to many basic emotions theories is that there should be functional signatures that distinguish different emotions: we should be able to tell what emotion a person is feeling by looking at his or her brain activity and/or physiology. Furthermore, knowledge of what the person is seeing or the larger context of the eliciting event should not be necessary to deduce what the person is feeling from observing the biological signatures. 

[5]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-ekman-5

On "constructionist" accounts, the emotion a person feels in response to a stimulus or event is "constructed" from more elemental biological and psychological ingredients. Two hypothesized ingredients are "core affect" (characterized by, e.g., hedonic 

valence

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_(psychology)

 and physiological arousal) and conceptual knowledge (such as the semantic meaning of the emotion labels themselves, e.g., the word "anger"). A theme common to many constructionist theories is that different emotions do not have specific locations in the nervous system or distinct physiological signatures, and that context is central to the emotion a person feels because of the accessibility of different concepts afforded by different contexts. 

[7]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-paradox-7

Dimensional models of emotion

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=3

]

For both theoretical and practical reasons, researchers define emotions according to one or more dimensions. In his 1649 philosophical treatise, 

The Passions of the Soul

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Passions_of_the_Soul

, Descartes defines and investigates the six primary passions ( 

Wonder

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonder_(emotion)

, 

love

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love

, 

hate

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate

, 

desire

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desire

, 

joy

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy

, and sadness). In 1897, 

Wilhelm Max Wundt

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Wundt

, the father of modern psychology, proposed that emotions can be described by three dimensions: "pleasurable versus unpleasurable", "arousing or subduing", and "strain or 

relaxation

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relaxation_(psychology)

". 

[8]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-8

 In 1954, 

Harold Schlosberg

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_H._Schlosberg

 named three dimensions of emotion: "pleasantness–unpleasantness", "attention–rejection" and "level of activation". 

[9]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-9

Dimensional models of emotion attempt to conceptualize human emotions by defining where they lie in two or three dimensions. Most dimensional models incorporate 

valence

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_(psychology)

 and 

arousal

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arousal

 or intensity dimensions. Dimensional models of emotion suggest that a common and interconnected neurophysiological system is responsible for all affective states. 

[10]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Posner_Russell_Peterson-10

 These models contrast theories of basic emotion, which propose that different emotions arise from separate neural systems. 

[10]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Posner_Russell_Peterson-10

 Several dimensional models of emotion have been developed, though there are just a few that remain as the dominant models currently accepted by most. 

[11]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Rubin_Telerico-11

 The two-dimensional models that are most prominent are the circumplex model, the vector model, and the Positive Activation – Negative Activation (PANA) model. 

[11]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Rubin_Telerico-11

Circumplex model

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=4

] 

Circumplex model of emotion has two axes: Valence and Arousal

The circumplex model of emotion was developed by James Russell. 

[12]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Russell1980-12

 This model suggests that emotions are distributed in a two-dimensional circular space, containing arousal and valence dimensions. Arousal represents the vertical axis and valence represents the horizontal axis, while the center of the circle represents a neutral valence and a medium level of arousal. 

[11]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Rubin_Telerico-11

 In this model, emotional states can be represented at any level of valence and arousal, or at a neutral level of one or both of these factors. Circumplex models have been used most commonly to test stimuli of emotion words, emotional facial expressions, and 

affective

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affect_(psychology)

 states. 

[13]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Remington-13

Russell and 

Lisa Feldman Barrett

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Feldman_Barrett

 describe their modified circumplex model as representative of core affect, or the most elementary feelings that are not necessarily directed toward anything. Different prototypical emotional episodes, or clear emotions that are evoked or directed by specific objects, can be plotted on the circumplex, according to their levels of arousal and 

pleasure

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleasure

. 

[14]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-14

Vector model

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=5

] 

The vector model of emotion suggests that emotions are structured in terms of arousal and valence. A positive valence represents appetitive motivation and negative valence represents defensive motivation. 

[15]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-15

The vector model of emotion appeared in 1992. 

[16]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Bradley-16

 This two-dimensional model consists of 

vectors

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space

 that point in two directions, representing a "boomerang" shape. The model assumes that there is always an underlying arousal dimension, and that valence determines the direction in which a particular emotion lies. For example, a positive valence would shift the emotion up the top vector and a negative valence would shift the emotion down the bottom vector. 

[11]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Rubin_Telerico-11

 In this model, high arousal states are differentiated by their valence, whereas low arousal states are more neutral and are represented near the meeting point of the vectors. Vector models have been most widely used in the testing of word and picture stimuli. 

[13]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Remington-13

Positive activation – negative activation (P.A.N.A.) model

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=6

]

The positive activation – negative activation (P.A.N.A.) or "consensual" model of emotion, originally created by Watson and Tellegen in 1985, 

[17]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Watson-17

 suggests that 

positive affect

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_affectivity

 and 

negative affect

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_affectivity

 are two separate systems. Similar to the vector model, states of higher arousal tend to be defined by their valence, and states of lower arousal tend to be more neutral in terms of valence. 

[11]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Rubin_Telerico-11

 In the P.A.N.A. model, the vertical axis represents low to high positive affect and the horizontal axis represents low to high negative affect. The dimensions of valence and arousal lay at a 45-degree rotation over these axes. 

[17]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Watson-17

Plutchik's model

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=7

]

Robert Plutchik

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Plutchik

 offers a three-dimensional model that is a hybrid of both basic-complex categories and dimensional theories. It arranges emotions in concentric circles where inner circles are more basic and outer circles more complex. Notably, outer circles are also formed by blending the inner circle emotions. Plutchik's model, as Russell's, emanates from a circumplex representation, where emotional words were plotted based on similarity. 

[18]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-18

 There are numerous emotions, which appear in several intensities and can be combined in various ways to form emotional "dyads". 

[19]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-19

 

[20]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-20

 

[21]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-21

 

[22]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Turner2000-22

 

[23]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-23

PAD emotional state model

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=8

]

Main article: 

PAD emotional state model

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PAD_emotional_state_model

The PAD emotional state model is a psychological model developed by 

Albert Mehrabian

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mehrabian

 and 

James A. Russell

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Russell

 to describe and measure emotional states. PAD uses three numerical dimensions to represent all emotions. 

[24]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Mehrabian1-24

 

[25]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-25

 The PAD dimensions are 

Pleasure

, 

Arousal

 and 

Dominance

.

The Pleasure-Displeasure Scale measures how pleasant an emotion may be. For instance, both anger and fear are unpleasant emotions, and score high on the displeasure scale. However, joy is a pleasant emotion. 

[24]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Mehrabian1-24

The Arousal-Nonarousal Scale measures how energized or soporific one feels. It is not the intensity of the emotion—for 

grief

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grief

 and 

depression

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(mood)

 can be low arousal intense feelings. While both anger and 

rage

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_(emotion)

 are unpleasant emotions, rage has a higher intensity or a higher arousal state. However 

boredom

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boredom

, which is also an unpleasant state, has a low arousal value. 

[24]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Mehrabian1-24

The Dominance-Submissiveness Scale represents the controlling and dominant nature of the emotion. For instance, while both fear and anger are unpleasant emotions, anger is a dominant emotion, while fear is a submissive emotion. 

[24]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Mehrabian1-24

Criticisms

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=9

]

Cultural considerations

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=10

]

Ethnographic and cross-cultural studies of emotions have shown the variety of ways in which emotions differ with cultures. Because of these differences, many cross-cultural psychologists and anthropologists challenge the idea of universal classifications of emotions altogether. Cultural differences have been observed in the way in which emotions are valued, expressed, and regulated. The social norms for emotions, such as the frequency with or circumstances in which they are expressed, also vary drastically. 

[26]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Mesquita-26

 

[27]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Russell1991-27

 For example, the demonstration of anger is encouraged by 

Kaluli people

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluli_people

, but condemned by Utku Inuit. 

[28]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Eid-28

The largest piece of evidence that disputes the universality of emotions is language. Differences within languages directly correlate to differences in emotion taxonomy. Languages differ in that they categorize emotions based on different components. Some may categorize by event types, whereas others categorize by action readiness. Furthermore, emotion taxonomies vary due to the differing implications emotions have in different languages. 

[26]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Mesquita-26

 That being said, not all English words have equivalents in all other languages and vice versa, indicating that there are words for emotions present in some languages but not in others. 

[29]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Wierzbicka-29

 Emotions such as the 

schadenfreude

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schadenfreude

 in German and 

saudade

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudade

 in Portuguese are commonly expressed in emotions in their respective languages, but lack an English equivalent.

Some languages do not differentiate between emotions that are considered to be the basic emotions in English. For instance, certain African languages have one word for both anger and sadness, and others for 

shame

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shame

 and fear. There is ethnographic evidence that even challenges the universality of the category "emotions" because certain cultures lack a specific word relating to the English word "emotions". 

[27]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Russell1991-27

Lists of emotions

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=11

]

Emotions are categorized into various affects, which correspond to the current situation. 

[30]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-30

 An affect is the range of feeling experienced. 

[31]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-31

 Both positive and negative emotions are needed in our daily lives. 

[32]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-32

 Many theories of emotion have been proposed, 

[33]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-33

 with contrasting views. 

[34]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-34

Basic emotions

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=12

]

William James

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_James

 in 1890 proposed four basic emotions: fear, grief, love, and rage, based on bodily involvement. 

[35]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-35

Paul Ekman

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Ekman

 identified six basic emotions: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise. 

[36]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Handel-36

 Wallace V. Friesen and 

Phoebe C. Ellsworth

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoebe_C._Ellsworth

 worked with him on the same basic structure. 

[37]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-37

 The emotions can be linked to facial expressions. In the 1990s, Ekman proposed an expanded list of basic emotions, including a range of positive and negative emotions that are not all encoded in facial muscles. 

[38]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Ekman_1999-38

 The newly included emotions are: 

amusement

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amusement

, 

contempt

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contempt

, 

contentment

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contentment

, 

embarrassment

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embarrassment

, excitement, 

guilt

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guilt_(emotion)

, pride in achievement, 

relief

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relief_(emotion)

, satisfaction, sensory pleasure, and shame. 

[38]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Ekman_1999-38

Richard and Bernice Lazarus

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Lazarus

 in 1996 expanded the list to 15 emotions: aesthetic experience, anger, 

anxiety

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anxiety

, 

compassion

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compassion

, depression, 

envy

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy

, fright, 

gratitude

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gratitude

, guilt, happiness, 

hope

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope

, 

jealousy

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jealousy

, love, 

pride

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride

, relief, sadness, and shame, in the book 

Passion and Reason

. 

[39]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-39

 

[40]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-40

Researchers 

[41]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-41

 at 

University of California, Berkeley

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley

 identified 27 categories of emotion: 

admiration

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiration

, 

adoration

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoration

, aesthetic appreciation, amusement, anger, anxiety, 

awe

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awe

, awkwardness, boredom, 

calmness

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calmness

, 

confusion

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confusion

, craving, disgust, 

empathic pain

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empathy

, entrancement, excitement, fear, 

horror

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear

, 

interest

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interest_(emotion)

, joy, 

nostalgia

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nostalgia

, relief, romance, sadness, satisfaction, sexual desire and surprise. 

[42]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-42

 This was based on 2185 short videos intended to elicit a certain emotion. These were then modeled onto a "map" of emotions. 

[43]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-43

Contrasting basic emotions

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=13

]

A 2009 review 

[44]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-44

 of theories of emotion identifies and contrasts fundamental emotions according to three key criteria for mental experiences that:

have a strongly motivating subjective quality like pleasure or pain;

are a response to some event or object that is either real or imagined;

motivate particular kinds of behavior.

The combination of these attributes distinguishes emotions from sensations, feelings and moods.

Emotion dynamics

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=14

]

Researchers distinguish several emotion dynamics, most commonly how intense (mean level), variable (fluctuations), inert (temporal dependency), instable (magnitude of moment-to-moment fluctuations), or differentiated someone's emotions are (the specificity of granularity of emotions), and whether and how an emotion augments or blunts other emotions. 

[45]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Reitsema,_A.M._2022_374%E2%80%93396-45

 Meta-analytic reviews show systematic developmental changes in emotion dynamics throughout childhood and adolescence and substantial between-person differences. 

[45]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Reitsema,_A.M._2022_374%E2%80%93396-45

Plutchik's wheel of emotions

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=17

] 

Plutchik's original emotion wheel 

A diagram depicting the primary, secondary, and tertiary dyads

In 1980, 

Robert Plutchik

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Plutchik

 diagrammed a wheel of eight emotions: joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger and 

anticipation

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticipation_(emotion)

, inspired by his 

Ten Postulates

. 

[49]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-49

 

[50]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-50

 Plutchik also theorized twenty-four "Primary", "Secondary", and "Tertiary" dyads (feelings composed of two emotions). 

[51]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-51

 

[52]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-Turner20002-52

 

[53]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-53

 

[54]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-auto-54

 

[55]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-55

 

[56]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-56

 

[57]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-57

 The wheel emotions can be paired in four groups:

Primary dyad = one petal apart = 

Love

 = 

Joy

 + 

Trust

Secondary dyad = two petals apart = 

Envy

 = 

Sadness

 + 

Anger

Tertiary dyad = three petals apart = 

Shame

 = 

Fear

 + 

Disgust

Opposite emotions = four petals apart = 

Anticipation

 ∉ 

Surprise

There are also triads, emotions formed from 3 primary emotions, though Plutchik never describes in any detail what the triads might be. 

[58]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-58

 This leads to a combination of 24 dyads and 32 triads, making 56 emotions at 1 intensity level. 

[59]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-59

 Emotions can be mild or intense; 

[60]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-60

 for example, distraction is a mild form of surprise, and rage is an intense form of anger. The kinds of relation between each pair of emotions are:

Similar emotions in the wheel are adjacent to each other. 

[61]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-61

 Anger, 

Anticipation

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticipation

, Joy, and Trust are positive in valence, while Fear, Surprise, Sadness, and Disgust are negative in valence. Anger is classified as a "positive" emotion because it involves "moving toward" a goal, 

[62]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-62

 while surprise is negative because it is a violation of someone's territory. 

[63]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-63

 The emotion dyads each have half-opposites and exact opposites: 

[64]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-64

[ 

edit

https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emotion_classification&action=edit&section=18

MIT

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology

 researchers 

[65]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion_classification#cite_note-interplay-65

 published a paper titled "An Affective Model of Interplay Between Emotions and Learning: Reengineering Educational Pedagogy—Building a Learning Companion" that lists six axes of emotions with different opposite emotions, and different emotions coming from ranges.

=== FIN_FUENTE ===

### FUENTE: Enhancing Discourse Dependency Parsing with Sentence Dependency Parsing: A Unified Generative Method Based on Code Representation - ACL Anthology ###
### TIPO: pdf | URL: https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.729.pdf | CARACTERES: 45377 ###
### KEYWORDS: Discourse Dependency Parsing, Large Language Models, Code Representation, Curriculum Learning, Sentence Dependency Parsing ###

Resumen: Researchers have developed a **unified generative method** to address the scarcity of data and inconsistent labeling in **Discourse Dependency Parsing (DDP)** by leveraging the structured reasoning of Large Language Models. This approach conceptualizes the parsing process as a **path-based search** represented through **code-based prompts**, which allows the model to utilize its inherent strengths in programming logic to map complex linguistic relationships. To further boost performance, the authors employ a **curriculum learning-based instruction tuning** strategy that bridges the gap between sentence-level and discourse-level tasks by training on increasingly difficult samples. Experimental results demonstrate that this **code-based representation** significantly outperforms traditional tuple-based methods, particularly in **low-resource scenarios** where training data is limited.

------

 

Enhancing Discourse Dependency Parsing with Sentence Dependency Parsing: A Unified Generative Method Based on Code Representation 

Zizhuo Shen and Yanqiu Shao∗ and Wei Li Beijing Language and Culture University, China 

blcushzz@gmail.com, yqshao163@163.com, liweitj47@blcu.edu.cn 

Abstract 

Due to the high complexity of Discourse De-pendency Parsing (DDP) tasks, their existing annotation resources are relatively scarce compared to other NLP tasks, and different DDP tasks also have significant differences in annotation schema. These issues have led to the dilemma of low resources for DDP tasks. Thanks to the powerful capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) in cross-task learning, we can use LLMs to model dependency parsing under different annotation schema in an unified manner, in order to alleviate the dilemma of low resources for DDP tasks. How-ever, enabling LLMs to deeply comprehend dependency parsing tasks is a challenge that remains underexplored. Inspired by the application of code-based methods in complex tasks, we propose a code-based unified dependency parsing method. We treat the process of dependency parsing as a search process of dependency paths and use code to represent this search process. Furthermore, we use a curriculum-learning based instruction tuning strategy for joint training of multiple dependency parsing tasks. The experimental results show that our proposed code-based DDP system has achieved good performance on two Chinese DDP tasks (especially significant improvement on the DDP task with relatively less training data). 

1 Introduction 

Discourse Dependency Parsing (DDP) is a structured prediction task. The input of this task is a sequence of Elementary Discourse Units (EDUs), and the output of this task is a dependency structure (a dependency tree labeled with discourse relation labels). As one of the fundamental tasks in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), DDP can assist downstream tasks such as emotion recognition (Ong et al., 2022), pronoun resolution (Yang 

∗Corresponding Author 

et al., 2021), and event relation extraction (Tang et al., 2021). 

Although the neural network-based NLP technology has greatly promoted the development of DDP tasks (Zhou and Feng, 2022; Liu et al., 2023). However, there are still some unresolved issues with DDP tasks. Firstly, the cost of annotating DDP data is relatively high, compared to Sentence-level Dependency Parsing (SDP) data, the existing scale of DDP data is smaller. Secondly, there are large differences in the annotation schema of DDP tasks, and heterogeneous data under different annotation schema are difficult to be effectively utilized (Nishida and Matsumoto, 2022). These problems have led to the dilemma of low resources in DDP tasks, limiting the application and development of DDP tasks. 

Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) has shown significant advantages in few-shot learning (Brown et al., 2020) and cross-task learning scenarios (Mishra et al., 2022) due to its powerful semantic understanding ability and transfer learning ability. Therefore, using LLM to design an unified dependency parsing method helps to break through the gap between dependency parsing tasks under different annotation granularity and different annotation schema, thereby overcoming the the dilemma of low resources in DDP tasks. 

However, how to more effectively use LLMs for dependency parsing tasks remains an issue that requires more attention. Specifically, we need to face challenges from the following two aspects. 

1. How to linearize dependency structures to suit the modeling method of language models? 

2. How to design unified and LLM-friendly prompts for dependency parsing tasks? 

For the first challenge, we propose a path decomposition-based strategy for linearizing dependency structures. Inspired by related work 

12497

on Chain of Thought technology (Wei et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023) in complex tasks, we treat the dependency parsing task as a step-by-step search process of dependency paths. The model needs to gradually search out the entire dependency structure from the root node according to some search order, such as depth-first search (DFS) or breadthfirst search (BFS). This strategy not only adapts to the modeling method of language models but also retains the structural information in the dependency structure. 

For the second challenge, inspired by LLM-related works in the field of information extraction (Li et al., 2023; Sainz et al., 2023). We proposed a code-based representation method for dependency parsing tasks. Firstly, we use code language to represent the basic elements in dependency parsing tasks. Specifically, we use variables to represent the sequence of semantic units and semantic relation labels; classes to represent dependency arcs and their constituent head nodes, dependent nodes, and dependency relations; functions to represent some specific operations in the process of dependency analysis. Then, based on these basic elements, we can transform the process of dependency parsing into the process of code execution. This method can not only use code language to describe the process of dependency parsing clearly and concisely but also leverage the powerful underlying code generation capability of LLMs. 

We attempt to model the SDP task and DDP task in an unified way, in order to achieve the goal of enhancing the DDP task using the SDP task. Specif-ically, we set the SDP task (we chose a syntactic dependency parsing task and a semantic dependency parsing task) as the source task, and set the DDP task as the target task. Leveraging our proposed dependency structure linearization strategy and the code-based dependency parsing task representation method, we are able to craft unified dependency parsing prompts for these tasks, and employ instruction tuning to equip LLMs with dependency parsing capabilities. 

To achieve better performance on DDP tasks, we further adopt a Curriculum Learning-based (CL-based) instruction tuning strategy. Specifically, we first calculate a difficulty value for each sample in the dependency parsing task based on prior features such as the type of dependency parsing task, the number of dependency paths, and the average 

depth of dependency paths. Then, we dynamically adjust the loss weight of each sample during the entire training process according to the difficulty value of the sample and the current training steps, so as to achieve a training mode that learns from simple samples first, and then learns from difficult samples. 

Our contributions can be summarized in the following three aspects: 1) we first propose to treat the dependency parsing process as a search process of dependency paths and design a code-based unified dependency parsing task prompt to represent this process. 2) We use a curriculum learning-based instruction tuning strategy to jointly train SDP tasks and DDP tasks, aiming to enhance the performance of DDP tasks with SDP tasks. 3) Our experimental results show that our code-based DDP system has achieved good performance in two Chinese DDP tasks, confirming the effectiveness of our proposed method. 

2 Approach 

Figure 1 illustrates code-based unified dependency parsing method we proposed. First, we give a definition of the unified dependency pasing task. Then, based on the path decomposition-based linearization strategy, we treat different types of dependency parsing tasks as the search process of dependency paths and use code-based prompt to represent this process. Finally, we propose a curriculum learning-based instruction tuning strategy to more effectively achieve the goal of using SDP tasks to improve DDP tasks. 

2.1 Formal Definition of Unified Dependency Parsing Tasks 

Given a sequence of semantic units U and a set of semantic relation labels L, the dependency parsing model needs to predict a set of dependency arcs A based on U and L. Each element ai = (hi, di, ri) in the dependency arc set A is a triplet. In the triplet, hi represents the head node of the dependency arc, di represents the dependent node of the dependency arc, and ri represents the dependency relation label. Among them, hi ∈ U , di ∈ U , ri ∈ L. The triples in the dependency arc set A can form the entire dependency structure D according to the linking relation.

2.2 Path Decomposition-based Linearization Strategy 

We regard the process of dependency parsing as a search process for dependency paths. For a given dependency structure, taking the root node as the starting node and through depth-first search or breadth-first search, we can transform it into a sequence P = {Pi} composed of several dependency paths. For any two adjacent dependency arcs ai = (hi, di, ri) and aj = (hj , dj , rj) in this sequence, they all satisfy the condition di = hj . 

Furthermore, through the path decomposition-based linearization strategy, we can model the task of dependency parsing as a structure-aware conditional language modeling task. For a given sequence of semantic units U and a set of semantic relation labels L, we can infer the dependency structure D through the following formula: 

D = argmax n∑ 

i 

logp(ai+1|ai, U, L) (1) 

2.3 Code-based Representation Method We use the concepts of variables, classes, and functions in the code language to design the code schema that can be used to represent dependency parsing tasks. Figure 2 shows the code schema we designed. 

Variables: We use the concept of variables to represent the semantic unit sequence and the set 

# Code Schema ## Variable index = "Index of a semantic unit" text = "Text of a semantic unit" label = "Label of a semantic relation" ## Class class Head(object): 

def __init__(self, index:str, text:str): self.index = index self.text = text 

class Dep(object): def __init__(self, index:str, text:str): 

self.index = index self.text = text 

class Rel(object): def __init__(self, label:str): 

self.label = label class Arc(object): 

def __init__(self, head:Head, dep:Dep, rel:Rel): self.head = head self.dep = dep self.rel = rel 

## Function def findRels(): 

return [label,] def searchPath(index:str): 

return def findArc(index:str): 

return Arc(Head(index, text), Dep(index, text), Rel(label)) def stop(): 

return 

Figure 2: The code schema that can be used to represent dependency parsing tasks. 

of semantic relation labels. The semantic unit sequence contains two parts of information, one part is the positional information of the semantic unit in the sequence, and the other part is the textual information of the semantic unit itself. For positional information, we use the variable name index to represent the positional index of the semantic unit, and the value range of this variable is 0 ∼ N , where N is the length of the semantic unit sequence. For textual information, we use the variable name text to represent it, and the value range of this variable is all texts of the semantic units in the sample. We use the variable name label to represent the label 

12499

of semantic relation. Classes: We use the concept of classes to repre-

sent the dependency arc and its components: head node, dependent node, and dependency relation. The head node is represented by the Head class, and the dependent node is represented by the Dep class. Both classes need to be instantiated with the index variable and text variable. The dependency relation is represented by the Rel class, which is instantiated by passing the label variable. The Arc class is used to represent the dependency arc, which is instantiated by passing the Head class, Dep class, and Arc class. 

Functions: We use the concept of functions to represent specific operations in the process of dependency parsing. The function findLabels is used to find all possible semantic relation labels between current semantic units, which takes no input and returns a set of semantic relation labels. The function searchPath is used to start searching for a new dependency path, which takes the position index of the starting semantic unit of the dependency path as input and has no return value. The function findArc is used to find a dependency arc, which takes the position index of the head node of the dependency arc as input and returns an instance of a dependency arc class. The function stop is used to indicate that all dependency paths in the dependency structure have been obtained, which takes neither input nor return value. 

2.4 Code-based Unified Dependency Parsing Task Prompt 

Figure 3 presents an example of the code-based unified dependency parsing task prompt. 

The input part of the prompt mainly includes the following sections of information: Task De-scription, Code Schema, Task Name, and Semantic Units. The Task Description section is a natural language explanation of the dependency parsing task. The Code Schema section contains all code languages needed in the process of dependency parsing. The Task Name indicates the type of dependency parsing task. The Semantic Units section contains position index information and text information of the semantic unit sequence, which we store in a dictionary data structure with the index as the key and the text information as the value. 

The output part of the prompt is the whole process of dependency parsing based on the current semantic unit. According to the example in Figure 

3, we can see that firstly, LLM needs to call the findLabels function to predict all possible semantic relation labels in the current sample. Then, LLM will call searchPath and findArc functions to predict all possible dependency paths in the current sample until the output of the stop function ends. 

2.5 Curriculum Learning-based Instruction Tuning 

To better utilize SDP tasks to enhance the performance of DDP tasks, we adopt a CL-based instruction tuning strategy for LLMs. Inspired by the work of (Elgaar and Amiri, 2023; Wang et al., 2022a), we implement a simple and effective instance-level weighting-based curriculum learning algorithm. 

Firstly, for each sample, we count several features: the type of dependency parsing task, the number of semantic units, the number of semantic relation labels, the number of dependency paths, and the average depth of dependency paths. For the type of dependency parsing task, we set the weight of syntactic dependency parsing task to 0.2, the weight of sentence-level semantic dependency parsing task to 0.3, and the weight of discourselevel dependency parsing task to 0.5. For the other features, we calculate the normalized value of each feature using formula 2, where Xi represents the value of a feature, Xmax represents the maximum value of that feature class, and Xmin represents the minimum value of that feature class. 

σi = Xi −Xmin 

Xmax −Xmin (2) 

Secondly, We calculate the average of all features for each sample using formula 3. This value can be regarded as the difficulty value of each sample. 

ϕj = 

∑n i σi n 

(3) 

Finally, we use the negative-sigmoid formula to calculate the weight of each sample throughout the entire training process. The input value of formula 4 is the difficulty value ϕj , the training progress p ∈ [0, 1], and a hyperparameter β ∈ [1,∞) that controls the rate of weight growth. 

wj = 1 

1 + exp(ϕj − p× β) (4) 

For a certain batch of samples, we can calculate the weighted loss through formula 5 for model

3 Experiments 

3.1 Datasets 

Sentence-level Dependency Parsing (SDP) Tasks: For sentence-level dependency parsing tasks, we chose a syntactic dependency parsing task and a semantic dependency parsing task for experiments. The dataset used for syntactic dependency parsing is Chinese Treebank 5.0 (CTB5), and the dataset used for semantic dependency parsing is Chinese Semantic Dependency Graph (CSDG) (Shao et al., 2023; Che et al., 2016). The basic information of these two datasets is shown in Table 1. 

Discourse-level Dependency Parsing (DDP) Tasks: For DDP tasks, we chose a DDP dataset based on news corpus (SU-CDTB) (Li et al., 2014) and a DDP dataset based on scientific paper abstracts (Sci-CDTB) (Cheng and Li, 2019) for exper-

iments. The basic information of these two datasets is shown in Table 1. 

3.2 Implementation Details 

We refer to the DDP system proposed in this work as the Code-based (if the system uses a curriculum learning-based instruction tuning strategy, we will refer it as Code-based + CL). In the main experiment, we primarily select baichuan2-7b-base 1 and deepseek-llm-7b-base 2, two 7B Base LLMs, to train our Code-based DDP System. Due to computational resource constraints, we adopt a QLoRA-based approach (Dettmers et al., 2023) for instruction tuning. The hyperparameters used during instruction tuning are as follows: learning_rate is 2e-4, lora_rank is 64, lora_alpha is 16, lora_dropout is 0.05, and the maximum number of epochs is 30. 

3.3 Baseline Systems 

In this work, the baseline systems we employ are categorized into three types: statistical machine learning-based (SML-based) systems, pre-trained language model-based (PLM-based) systems, and LLM-based systems. 

SML-based Systems: We mainly compare the SML-based methods used in previous work. Graph-based System (Li et al., 2014) utilizes a perceptron-based algorithm to implement the DDP system. Vanilla Transition-based System (Nivre, 2003) uses an SVM-based model to predict transition actions and achieve DDP. Two-stage Transition-based System(Wang et al., 2017) initially uses an SVM-based model to predict transi-

tion actions for the prediction of dependency structures, followed by another SVM-based model to accomplish the prediction of dependency relations. 

PLM-based Systems: We select some opensource PLM-based DDP systems as baselines. BERT-based Two-stage System (Zhou and Feng, 2022) is a two-stage transition-based DDP system. This system first uses a transition-based model (BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) is used for the extraction of transition system state features) to predict dependency structures, and then uses a BERT-based sequence labeling model to predict dependency relations. BERT-based Biaffine System (Nishida and Matsumoto, 2022) is a classic graph-based DDP system. This system uses BERT to extract EDU features and uses Biaffine networks (Dozat and Manning, 2017) to predict dependency structures and dependency relations. DAMT-based System (Fan et al., 2022) is a DDP system that uses a multi-task learning method. This system combines the advantages of transition-based DDP systems and graph-based DDP systems, and uses XLNet (Yang et al., 2019) to extract EDU features. 

LLM-based Systems: To verify the effectiveness of the code-based DDP system proposed in this paper, we implement a Tuple-based DDP system. The input of the tuple-based DDP system is the semantic unit of the current sample, and the output is the collection of all possible dependency relation tuples in the current sample. Each dependency relation tuple is represented in the form of a five-tuple: (head node semantic unit index, head node semantic unit text, dependent node semantic unit index, dependent node semantic unit text, semantic relation label). 

3.4 Main Results 

According to the experimental results in Table 2, we can draw several conclusions. 

The code-based DDP system has achieved competitive results on DDP tasks. On the SU-CDTB test set with more training samples, the 

code-based DDP system has reached a level comparable to multiple PLM-based DDP systems. On the Sci-CDTB test set with fewer training samples, the effect of the code-based DDP system has surpassed that of the PLM-based DDP system. These experimental results indicate that the code-based DDP system may have a better ability to learn from small scale samples. 

The code-based DDP system performs better than the tuple-based DDP system on DDP tasks. In several experiments based on LLM, whether using baichuan2-7b-base or deepseek-llm-7b-base, the code-based DDP system performs better than the tuple-based DDP system on both test sets. These experimental results suggest that LLM might more easily understand data in code form, and the structural information in the code-based DDP system may help improve the performance of DDP. 

Introducing SDP tasks and performing CL-based instruction tuning can significantly improve the performance of code-based DDP systems. These experimental results indicate that SDP tasks have a positive effect on DDP tasks. Fur-thermore, we believe that the unified dependency parsing task prompt build a bridge between different forms of dependency parsing tasks, enabling LLM to learn the common features of dependency parsing tasks from different dependency parsing tasks, thereby realizing cross-task transfer. 

3.5 Detailed Analysis 

Comparison of Different Instruction Tuning Strategies: To verify the effectiveness of the CL-based instruction tuning strategy, we implement two additional instruction tuning strategies for comparative experiments. 

The first is multi-task learning-based (MTL-based) instruction tuning. Under this strategy, we merge the training data of all tasks together for training. Throughout the training process, we do not adjust the weight of each sample’s loss based

Then, based on the model obtained from the first stage of training, we perform the second stage of training on DDP tasks. 

According to the experimental results in Table 3, we find that the CL-based instruction tuning strategy outperforms the other two instruction tuning strategies on both test sets. These experimental results indicate that the CL-based instruction tuning strategy can better enhance the LLM’s learning of DDP tasks, thereby effectively avoiding multi-task conflicts, catastrophic forgetting, and other problems present in the other two training methods. 

Comparison of Different Types of Models: In order to compare the effects of different types of LLMs on DDP tasks, we chose several different types of LLMs released by DeepSeek to train Code-based DDP systems and conduct a comparative analysis. The deepseek-llm-7b-base model (Base Model) is trained from scratch on a vast dataset 

of 2T tokens in both English and Chinese. The deepseek-llm-7b-chat model (Chat Model) 3 is initialized from deepseek-llm-7b-base and fine-tuned on extra instruction data. The deepseek-coder-7b-instruct model (Code Model) 4 is initialized from deepseek-llm-7b-base and fine-tuned on extra code data and instruction data. 

According to the experimental results in Figure 4, firstly, we find that the performance of Code model and Base model on DDP tasks is significantly better than that of Chat model. This indicates that the Chat model has lost a certain degree of code ability after enhancing its dialogue ability. Secondly, although the Code model performs slightly worse than the Base model on the SU-CDTB test set, the Code model’s performance on the Sci-CDTB test set is significantly better than the Base model. This suggests that further enhancing the code ability of LLM can help improve the performance of Code-based DDP on DDP tasks, especially on tasks with relatively less training data. 

Comparison of Different Linearization Or-ders: To compare the effects of data obtained from different linearization orders on DDP tasks, we use data obtained from DFS linearization, BFS linearization, and a mixture of DFS and BFS linearization to train Code-based DDP systems. 

According to the experimental results in Figure 5, we find that whether the data obtained by using the DFS linearization or the BFS linearization, the performance of the Code-based DDP system on

4 Related Works 

Dependency parsing: Common dependency parsing methods can be divided into three categories: graph-based methods (Dozat and Manning, 2017, 2018; Zhang et al., 2020), transition-based methods (Wang et al., 2022b; Zhou and Feng, 2022), and autoregressive generative methods (Li et al., 2018; He and Choi, 2023). The graph-based method treats the dependency parsing task as a graph search prob-

lem. This method requires a scoring model to calculate the scores of each edge in the dependency structure. The transition-based method treats the dependency parsing task as a sequence-to-action conversion problem (Sun et al., 2022). This method usually requires different transition systems to be designed for different types of dependency structures. The autoregressive generative method treats the dependency parsing task as a sequence-to-sequence generation problem. This method usually requires linearizing the dependency structure to fit the modeling method of autoregressive generative models. Thanks to the powerful generation capabilities of LLMs, we also try to use the autoregressive generative method to build our dependency parsing system. Unlike previous work, we first attempt to use code to represent different types of dependency parsing tasks, and use a curriculum-learning based instruction tuning strategy for joint training of multiple dependency parsing tasks. 

Code-based Methods for NLP: Given that LLMs are typically pre-trained using code data and have developed strong capabilities in code comprehension and generation, consequently, some researchers have embarked on exploring the use of code for complex NLP tasks, aiming to harness the inherent code processing strengths of LLMs. Wang et al. (2023) use code language to represent event extraction tasks, improving the performance of LLM in event extraction tasks. Bi et al. (2023) use code language to represent triple extraction tasks for automatic construction of knowledge graphs. Li et al. (2024) propose a code-based unified information extraction method and verifiy the effectiveness of this method in few-shot learning scenarios and instruction tuning scenarios. Inspired by above works, we first try to use code language to represent more complex dependency paring tasks. 

5 Conclusion 

In order to better utilize LLMs to alleviate the low-resource dilemma of DDP tasks, we propose a code-based unifed dependency parsing method. Specifically, we regard the process of dependency parsing as a search process of dependency paths and design a code-based unifed dependency parsing task prompt based on this search process. Fur-thermore, we use a curriculum learning-based instruction tuning strategy to jointly train SDP tasks and DDP tasks under different annotation shema, achieving the goal of using SDP tasks to enhance

Limitations 

The main limitations of our research include the following aspects: 1) Computational resource limitations. When selecting models, we only consider models with a parameter size of 7B for testing, without exploring models with larger parameter sizes; in terms of training strategies, we only adopt the parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, without attempting the full parameter fine-tuning method. 2) Test set limitations. Our experiments only involved two representative Chinese DDP test sets, without extending to more languages or domains. 3) Experimental scenario limitations. We only verify the effectiveness of the proposed method in the supervised fine-tuning scenario, without conducting experiments in the in-context learning scenario. 

We plan to conduct experiments on more models and test sets in future work and verify the effectiveness of our proposed method in the in-context learning scenario.

### KEYWORDS: Hyperdimensional Computing, Wearable Biosignal Classification, Alcohol Intoxication Detection, Resource-Efficient Edge AI, Hybrid Symbolic-Classical Models ###

Resumen: This bachelor's thesis investigates the efficacy of **Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC)** as a brain-inspired, symbolic framework for the real-time classification of **physiological biosignals** via wearable devices. Conducted as a collaboration between UPC and UC Irvine, the research specifically targets the detection of **alcohol intoxication** by processing motion and heart rate data into high-dimensional vectors that are computationally efficient and robust to noise. The author systematically compares **standalone HDC variants**, traditional **deep learning architectures** like CNNs and LSTMs, and **hybrid models** that pair symbolic encoders with classical machine learning classifiers. By benchmarking these approaches against metrics such as **energy consumption, latency, and memory footprint**, the study highlights how HDC-based systems can enable **resource-efficient edge AI** for sustainable health monitoring. Ultimately, the work identifies specific hybrid configurations as the most viable solutions for deploying transparent and lightweight diagnostic tools on hardware-constrained smartwatches.

Abstract 

This thesis investigates the use of Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) for real-time classification of physiological signals, targeting intoxication detection from wearable biosensors. A unified evaluation framework is used to benchmark classical deep learning models, standalone HDC variants, and hybrid HDC-classical architectures. These models are assessed across accuracy, latency, memory footprint, energy efficiency, and interpretability. An application-driven pruning process identifies MAP, MAP+XGBoost, and MAP+LightGBM as the most viable candidates. The results show promise of symbolic representations in enabling efficient, transparent, and deployable edge AI for physiological time series analysis. 

Keywords: Hyperdimensional Computing · Wearable AI · Time Series Classification · Edge Inference · Model Efficiency · Physiological Signals

Chapter 1 

Introduction 

“The point of all this is to find a representation that simplifies computation.” 

— Pentti Kanerva, summarizing HDC in one line 

This thesis was conducted as part of an applied research collaboration between the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC) and the University of California, Irvine (UCI), under the Balsells Fellowship Program. Hosted at UCI, the work explores how brain-inspired symbolic representations, specifically hyperdimensional computing (HDC), can be used to model physiological time series in wearable alcohol detection systems. The resulting models were designed, evaluated, and benchmarked entirely in a resourceconstrained local setting, simulating the requirements of embedded, real-time operation. 

When I first joined this project, the goal was already well-defined and impactful: using smartwatch data to detect alcohol intoxication. A functioning system had been developed at UCI using deep learning methods and engineered features. My role was to build upon this foundation by refining the pipeline, enhancing its robustness, and optimizing it for lightweight, real-time deployment. 

As I progressed with the data and model analysis, it became clear that the task provided a valuable opportunity to compare distinct approaches to artificial intelligence. Tra-ditional neural networks offered strong predictive capabilities but were computationally intensive and difficult to interpret. In contrast, hyperdimensional computing (HDC) presented a lightweight, symbolic alternative that encodes information as high-dimensional vectors and operates through algebraic manipulation. This contrast allowed for a systematic evaluation of performance, efficiency, and interpretability across both paradigms. 

Over time, the scope of the thesis expanded into a structured comparative study of these two paradigms. It evaluates whether hyperdimensional computing (HDC), known for its lightweight and hardware-efficient properties, can match or complement classical machine learning (ML) and deep learning models in the context of real-world physiological signal classification. Additionally, it examines whether integrating HDC with conventional classifiers can enhance generalization and predictive performance while maintaining the transparency and efficiency that characterize HDC. 

Along the way, I built a unified benchmarking framework that treats all models, classical, symbolic, and hybrid, using the same preprocessing, training, and deployment conditions. This approach not only enables direct comparison but also provides a reproducible pipeline that can be extended and reused in future research within the lab. 

The work also aligns with broader goals in sustainable AI. Models were benchmarked for inference time, energy consumption, RAM usage, and model size, all measured lo-

1

cally without GPU acceleration. Several HDC variants were implemented, including Binary Spatter Code (BSC), Holographic Reduced Representation (HRR), Fourier HRR (FHRR), and Multiply-Accumulate-Permute (MAP). These were compared to classical architectures like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs), and to hybrid approaches that combine symbolic encoders with classifiers such as support vector machines (SVMs), random forests (RFs), and extreme gradient boosting (XGB). 

Although the models were evaluated on a relatively small, real-world dataset, the findings provide broader insights into the role of symbolic computing within modern AI pipelines, particularly in resource-constrained wearable applications where latency and energy efficiency are critical. 

The remainder of this thesis is structured as follows: 

 Chapter 2 provides background on wearable physiological sensing, time series classification, and HDC, along with a review of related work and a clear statement of objectives and research questions. 

 Chapter 3 presents the initial planning stage, including technical setup, infrastructure, risk assessment, cost analysis, and sustainability considerations. 

 Chapter 4 introduces the theoretical foundations of HDC, details its vector space operations, and describes the encoding pipeline used for physiological signal processing in this study. 

 Chapter 5 outlines the modeling objectives, experimental design, benchmarking strategy, and considerations for real-world deployment and reproducibility. 

 Chapter 6 presents the implementation, evaluation, and deployment benchmarking of baseline deep learning models, including Bi-LSTM, CNN, GRU, and LSTM. 

 Chapter 7 applies the same evaluation framework to standalone HDC models, examining how different symbolic vector space formulations (BSC, HRR, FHRR, and MAP), impact classification performance and deployability. 

 Chapter 8 extends the analysis to hybrid architectures that combine fixed HDC encoders with classical classifiers. Evaluated combinations include MAP+RF, MAP+SVM, MAP+MLP, MAP+XGB, and MAP+LightGBM. This chapter assesses whether decoupling symbolic encoding from decision-making improves generalization, flexibility, and deployment efficiency. 

 Chapter 9 synthesizes the results through comparative trade-off analyses, identifies top-performing models, addresses the research questions, and reflects on lessons learned, limitations, and future work. 

 The Appendix includes supporting materials such as the Gantt chart, radar plot construction, detailed metrics, and implementation artifacts. 

2

Chapter 2 

Context and Scope 

This chapter reviews background terms and concepts, examines the current state of the art, and outlines the objectives and research questions, establishing the context for the research. 

2.1 Background 

2.1.1 Wearable and Physiological Sensing 

Wearable devices have become an essential part of how we monitor physiological 

and behavioral signals in everyday life [1]. Modern smartwatches and fitness trackers are typically equipped with sensors like accelerometers and gyroscopes to track movement and orientation, as well as photoplethysmography (PPG) sensors to estimate heart rate [2]. These sensors offer high-frequency, non-invasive measurements and are well suited for long-term monitoring, which makes them ideal for modeling time series data [3]. 

Physiological data collected from wearable devices have been applied in a wide range of use cases, including activity recognition, stress and sleep monitoring, and the prediction of health-related events [4]. More recently, these signals have also been investigated as indirect indicators of substance use and cognitive state [5]–[7]. 

In this thesis, the models are trained using sensor data collected from participants wearing smartwatches that measure both motion and cardiovascular activity. A separate alcohol biosensor was also used to capture Transdermal Alcohol Concentration (TAC); however, this signal was not included as a model input. Instead, it served to label each session as either intoxicated or sober. This setup enables the development of models that rely exclusively on wearable signals to infer user state, eliminating the need for dedicated chemical sensors [8]. 

2.1.2 Time Series Classification 

Time series classification (TSC) involves assigning a discrete label to sequences of 

data that are ordered in time. In wearable computing, this typically means working with physiological signals such as acceleration, gyroscopic movement, and heart rate, which is data that evolve continuously and exhibit both short-term variations and long-range dependencies [9], [10]. TSC presents several challenges, including temporal misalignment, noise, and variability between individuals [11]. 

3

Traditional approaches to time series classification include similarity-based methods like k-Nearest Neighbors with Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), as well as feature-based techniques that extract statistical descriptors from fixed windows of time series data. 

More recent research has shifted toward deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and Transformer architectures. These models are capable of automatically learning hierarchical temporal patterns, but they often require significant computational resources, large amounts of labeled data, and complex training pipelines. As a result, their use in real-time, lowpower settings like wearable devices remains limited [12]. 

HDC provides an alternative that balances simplicity, efficiency, and robustness. It encodes temporal sequences as high-dimensional vectors using operations such as binding, permutation, and superposition, enabling symbolic representation of time-dependent information. HDC supports online learning, requires little to no parameter tuning, and is well suited for resource-constrained environments [13]. 

In this thesis, the time series classification problem is formulated as a binary task to infer the user’s intoxication state using physiological data collected from a wearable device. Transdermal Alcohol Concentration (TAC) readings are used to generate ground-truth labels through thresholding, enabling supervised training. The model itself is designed to operate solely on motion and heart rate signals during inference [14], [15]. 

2.1.3 Hyperdimensional Computing 

HDC is a brain-inspired paradigm that encodes information as high-dimensional vec-

tors and processes it using symbolic algebraic operations. Its simplicity, noise robustness, and low computational cost make it a strong candidate for resource-constrained environments like wearables [13], [16]. 

A full explanation of HDC principles, vector space formulations, and the encoding pipeline used in this thesis is provided in Chapter 4. 

2.1.4 Machine Learning on Embedded Devices 

Machine learning models are increasingly deployed on embedded platforms such as 

smartwatches, smartphones, and microcontroller-based wearables. These devices support real-time, on-device inference for applications like activity recognition and health monitoring [17]. However, they come with strict limitations on memory, computation, and power, which can challenge the deployment of conventional model architectures [18]. 

In this context, classical models such as decision trees, support vector machines, and k nearest neighbors are often preferred due to their simplicity and low overhead. While effective on small datasets and easy to interpret [19], these methods generally require manual feature engineering and may struggle to capture the complex temporal dynamics of physiological signals [20]. 

Deep learning models have demonstrated strong performance in time series classification and multivariate sensor analysis. Their ability to learn hierarchical and temporal representations makes them attractive for modeling sequential physiological data [21], [22]. Nevertheless, these models are often memory-intensive and require significant training resources, making them more challenging to deploy on low-power devices without model compression or hardware acceleration [23]. 

4

2.2 State of the Art 

2.2.1 Transdermal Alcohol Detection and Wearable Sensing 

Transdermal alcohol detection provides a non-invasive alternative to breathalyzers 

and blood tests by estimating ethanol excretion through the skin [24]. Devices such as the BACtrack Skyn use electrochemical sensors embedded in wristbands to monitor TAC at minute-level resolution during daily activities [25]. 

Prior studies have leveraged TAC data to track drinking episodes [26], compare it to self-reported consumption [27], and calibrate its lag relative to Blood Alcohol Concen-tration (BAC) [28], [29]. More recent work combines TAC with physiological signals for predictive modeling [30]. 

This thesis builds on these efforts by exploring whether intoxication detection can be achieved using only motion and heart rate data from commodity smartwatches, eliminating the need for specialized TAC sensors at inference time. 

2.2.2 Time Series Classification in Wearable Sensing 

TSC is widely used in wearable computing to infer states such as activity, stress, 

or cardiovascular health from physiological signals like acceleration, gyroscopic motion, and heart rate. Early methods relied on techniques like k-Nearest Neighbors with Dy-namic Time Warping (DTW) or handcrafted feature extraction paired with classical classifiers [31], [32]. 

Deep learning approaches have since become popular for their ability to capture complex temporal dependencies [33], [34]. However, their high resource demands make them difficult to deploy on embedded devices without model compression or specialized hardware [23], [35]. 

2.2.3 Hyperdimensional Computing in Classification 

Recent efforts in our lab have explored HDC as a resource-efficient alternative for phys-

iological signal classification on wearable platforms [14], [36]. These studies demonstrated that HDC-based models, when applied to motion and heart rate data, can achieve competitive accuracy while requiring significantly less memory and computation than deep learning approaches. 

Beyond intoxication detection, HDC has shown promise in related time series tasks such as EMG-based gesture recognition [37], language identification [38], and biosignal analysis [39]. Hybrid pipelines that combine symbolic HDC encoders with trainable classifiers have also been proposed to improve flexibility and performance [40], although their use in wearable sensing contexts remains underexplored. 

This thesis expands on that foundation by systematically evaluating different HDC vector space designs and hybrid configurations under real-world deployment constraints. 

5

2.3 Objective, Research Questions, and Scope 

2.3.1 Objective 

This thesis began as an applied effort to enhance the performance and deployment 

readiness of an existing intoxication detection pipeline developed at UCI. The pipeline uses wearable sensor data, specifically, motion and heart rate signals, to classify intoxication states, with TAC as the source of ground-truth labels. 

Initial contributions centered on refining preprocessing routines and improving the robustness of model training. However, the project evolved into a broader investigation into the design space of HDC for time series classification. In particular, this work examines how different vector space formulations; BSC, HRR, FHRR, and MAP, influence performance, interpretability, and deployment cost. 

Additionally, the thesis explores hybrid pipelines in which symbolic HDC encoders are decoupled from the decision layer, allowing downstream classifiers to process fixed hypervectors. These architectures are benchmarked not only for predictive accuracy, but also for their memory usage, inference latency, and energy efficiency. 

The main objectives are: 

 

Practical Objective: 

Improve the modeling and preprocessing pipeline of a wearable-based alcohol detection system by enhancing robustness, modularity, and classification performance. 

 

Scientific Objective: 

Systematically evaluate how different HDC vector space representations impact the effectiveness of symbolic encoding in time series classification tasks. 

 

Architectural Objective: 

Investigate the benefits of hybrid symbolic-classical models that pair HDC encoders with trainable classifiers, and assess their ability to capture non-linear patterns. 

 

Deployment Objective: 

Analyze the computational and memory efficiency of both standalone and hybrid HDC models to assess their feasibility for edge deployment. 

 

Empirical Gap Addressed: 

Contribute a comprehensive, reproducible benchmarking study of HDC models on real-world, noisy physiological time series, an area still underexplored in existing literature. 

2.3.2 Research Questions 

This work is guided by the following research questions: 

1. 

Vector Spaces: 

How do different HDC vector spaces (BSC, HRR, FHRR, MAP) compare in terms of classification accuracy, interpretability, and robustness on multivariate physiological time series? 

2. 

Hybrid Architectures: 

Can hybrid models, where symbolic hypervectors are fed into classical classifiers, improve predictive performance or generalization compared to prototype-based HDC inference? 

6

3. 

Comparative Modeling: 

How do HDC-based models (standalone and hybrid) compare to classical ML and deep learning approaches when trained and evaluated under the same preprocessing and cross-validation setup? 

4. 

Deployment Feasibility: 

What are the practical trade-offs (inference time, energy use, memory footprint) involved in deploying HDC models on resource-constrained devices, and how do these vary across variants? 

5. 

Pipeline Validity: 

Does the unified, symbolically encoded pipeline maintain generality and robustness across modeling families, and can it support reproducible evaluation for future physiological sensing applications? 

2.3.3 Scope 

This thesis focuses on end-to-end symbolic modeling of physiological time series for 

intoxication detection using wearable sensors. It restricts inference to real-time observable signals (accelerometer and heart rate) and uses TAC solely for offline binary labeling of windows. The scope includes: 

 Preprocessing and synchronization of wearable sensor data, including signal alignment, windowing, and artifact handling. 

 A common symbolic encoding framework using HDC, applied uniformly across multiple vector spaces and classifier combinations. 

 Design and evaluation of both standalone HDC classifiers and hybrid pipelines incorporating downstream classical ML models. 

 Performance benchmarking against classical baselines under controlled, reproducible conditions. 

 Deployment benchmarking, including metrics on latency, memory usage, RAM impact, and energy efficiency. 

The project is grounded in a real-world dataset collected through a field study at UCI. While this dataset includes wearable hardware and participant compensation, this thesis focuses exclusively on model development and comparative evaluation, not on data acquisition or clinical outcome analysis.
