Map-Like Representations of an Abstract Conceptual Space in the Human Brain

L B Levan Bokeria *

https://loop.frontiersin.org/people/1093727

R N Richard N. Henson

https://loop.frontiersin.org/people/9458

R M Robert M. Mok *

https://loop.frontiersin.org/people/36166

MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Article metrics

View details

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#metrics

3

Citations

7,1k

Views

1,8k

Downloads

Introduction

Much of higher cognition involves abstracting away from sensory details and thinking conceptually. How do our brains learn and represent such abstract concepts? Recent work has proposed that neural representations in the medial temporal lobe (MTL), which are involved in spatial navigation, might also support learning of higher-level knowledge structures (Behrens et al., 2018 ; Bellmund et al., 2018 ). Under this view, a range of MTL neurons such as place cells, grid cells, and head-direction cells may support the ability to mentally “navigate” through conceptual spaces. This extends the original proposal by Tolman ( 1948 ) that people construct “cognitive maps” that support broad psychological functions, and offers the exciting potential of understanding the cognitive processes that underlie category learning, reinforcement learning, and spatial navigation under a single unified framework.

These ideas are supported by findings that neural representations in the MTL, as well as the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), are involved in “navigation” of simple two-dimensional spaces of visual stimuli (Constantinescu et al., 2016 ; Theves et al., 2019 , 2020 ), social spaces (Tavares et al., 2015 ; Park et al., 2020 ), and odor spaces (Bao et al., 2019 ). A recent study in the Journal of Neuroscience (Viganò and Piazza, 2020 ) takes this research further by suggesting that the entorhinal cortex (EHC) and the mPFC are capable of mapping not only sensory spaces, but also abstract semantic spaces. In this opinion piece, we first describe the paradigm and results of Viganò and Piazza ( 2020 ), as well as the importance of their findings for the field. We then raise several methodological concerns and suggest changes to the paradigm to address these issues. Finally, we discuss potential future research directions including experimental and modeling approaches to tackle outstanding questions in the field.

Experimental Paradigm and Results

Viganò and Piazza ( 2020 ) employed a two-dimensional, multisensory space, in which each exemplar was characterized by the size of a visual image and the pitch of a concurrent auditory tone ( 

Figures 1A,B

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

). To assess how the brain organizes category knowledge in this space, they used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure the distances and directions between the neural representations of exemplars, both before and after category learning. The experiment involved three phases: (1) a pre-learning fMRI task, (2) nine days of behavioral training on the category structure, and (3) a post-learning fMRI task. During pre-learning, participants performed a 1-back stimulus identity task on the exemplars and on verbal labels (the pseudowords KER, MOS, DUN, and GAL) that denoted the four later-to-be-learned categories ( 

Figure 1B

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

). During behavioral training, participants learned to map each exemplar to one of the four categories. The post-learning task was similar to the pre-learning task, except participants performed a 1-back category identity task, responding whenever an exemplar was followed by its corresponding category label or vice versa.

Figure 1

Task and results summary. 

(A)

 An example audiovisual object used in the experiment. Each object was of a particular size and made a sound of a specific pitch as it visually compressed on the screen. 

(B)

 Left: Illustration of the 16 objects in a 2D audiovisual sensory space defined by size and pitch. Right: Objects were assigned one of four category labels (meaningless pseudowords), which defined the abstract semantic/category space on top of the sensory space. Objects marked with white and gray circles were both used in the behavioral sessions; only the ones marked in gray were used in the fMRI sessions. 

(C,D)

 Brain representations coding semantic distance. 

(C)

 Left: Illustration of greater distances in semantic space between diagonal categories (here KER—GAL) than non-diagonal distances (here KER—MOS). Right: Whole-brain fMRI-adaptation analysis performed on post-learning data revealed a significant cluster in the mPFC. 

(D)

 Left: Representational similarity analysis (RSA) using a model based on distances between categories. Right: Whole-brain RSA searchlight revealed a significant cluster in the mPFC. 

(E)

 Grid-like representations of semantic space. Left: Assuming a grid-like representation in semantic space, a specific pattern of activation across different movement directions should be expected (where movement refers to transitions between stimuli on successive trials). A grid-model dissimilarity matrix represents the predicted pairwise dissimilarities between voxel activity patterns evoked by the different directions as a function of their angular distance in 60° periodic space. This grid-model is then correlated with the voxel activity patterns evoked by the different movement directions to reveal the presence of a grid-like response. Right: whole-brain searchlight results using the model-based grid-RSA. Maps are thresholded at 

p

 < 0.05 uncorrected for visualization. Bar plot inset shows the average dissimilarity between activity patterns evoked by different directions in the entorhinal cortex, varying as a function of angular distance modulo 60. The figure is adapted from Viganò and Piazza ( 2020 ), 

Journal of Neuroscience

.

When searching for neural representations that related to the distances between categories, the authors utilized the fact that diagonal category pairs (such as DUN-MOS) differed in both dimensions and so were further apart than horizontal/vertical categories (such as KER-MOS) that differed in only one dimension ( 

Figure 1C

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

, left). They used fMRI-adaptation to detect sensitivity to small vs. large distances, and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to assess similarity between neural representations across categories ( 

Figure 1D

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

, left). Both analyses revealed a significant cluster in the mPFC that reflected greater distance between diagonal categories than horizontal/vertical categories post-learning, but not pre-learning ( 

Figures 1C,D

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

). An additional fMRI-adaptation analysis focusing on the EHC showed that the EHC also tracked category distances. Importantly, a control RSA based on distances between individual exemplars suggested that the mPFC was not sensitive to sensory distances between stimuli either pre- or post-learning, demonstrating its specificity to the more abstract category space.

The authors then used model-based RSA to test for direction-based grid-like neural codes for “movement” across the category space. A model was constructed to reflect the predicted similarities between all eight possible movement directions in the category space (“moving” from one trial to the next in the 1-back task). The similarities across directions were calculated assuming a 6-fold periodicity that would result from using a grid-like code ( 

Figure 1E

, left; see Bellmund et al., 2016 ; though note that only eight directions were sampled in this study). A whole-brain searchlight revealed a cluster in the right EHC consistent with this model ( 

Figure 1E

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

, right). This EHC signal was not sensitive to 4, 5, and 7-fold periodicities, and was only present post-learning. Notably, the authors did not find a direction-modulated signal in the mPFC.

Together, these results suggest that the neural mechanisms that underlie spatial processing are recycled to represent not just sensory spaces but also more abstract category spaces. Specifically, the mPFC and the EHC represent category distances, and the EHC tracks the movement directions in that space, possibly using the same grid-like codes found in spatial navigation tasks.

Discussion

Despite its innovative paradigm, aspects of the experimental design warrant further consideration. Specifically, the pre- vs. post-learning tasks differed in nature (1-back stimulus identity vs. 1-back category identity), which could have introduced confounds such as differences in task difficulty—i.e., greater brain activity due to higher cognitive demand in the category task. This is one reason why the authors did not report a direct pre- vs. post-learning whole-brain comparison, even though such a contrast revealed the same mPFC cluster as reported in the paper (personal communication, April 9, 2020). One way to address this issue would be to run the 1-back stimulus identity task post- as well as pre-learning, attributing any changes in brain activity to the newly acquired category knowledge. This would allow a direct whole-brain comparison between pre- and post-learning stages, providing a better and more comprehensive test compared to the pre- post-learning comparison within the mPFC ROI identified by the analysis after learning ( 

Figures 1C,D

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

, right; also see Viganò and Piazza, 2020 , Figures 2C,F). Indeed, the authors did run a post-learning 1-back stimulus identity task, but with fewer number of runs than pre-learning, undermining the power of the pre-post contrast (personal communication, April 9, 2020). Additionally, a post-learning 1-back stimulus identity task might not have activated the learned category knowledge since it is not required to perform the task. Thus, an alternative approach would be to introduce a within-participant “no-learning” control condition, where participants perform a pre-learning 1-back stimulus identity task and a post-learning 1-back category identity task on a second, distinct set of stimuli and category labels. Crucially, participants would not learn category-to-exemplar mappings in between the tasks (such that in the post-learning task, participants would need to guess the category to which exemplars belong). Then, one could examine distance and direction sensitivity that was unique to the “learned” space.

Another issue concerns the possibility that the direction-based, grid-like representations of concept space may be partially driven by more concept-level overlap in one direction than others. With four categories arranged in a square format, only a subset of directions across concepts could be sampled (0–315° in 45° steps), thereby omitting several key directions (60° and 120°) when testing for a 6-fold periodic signal ( 

Figure 1E

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

, left). Therefore, the significant correlation with the grid-model could have been mainly driven by the higher pattern similarity (lower dissimilarity) in the 180° direction. The issue is that the conditions that are compared in the 180° direction contained stimuli that shared two concept labels (e.g., DUN→GAL then GAL→DUN) whereas the other direction conditions only shared one concept label (e.g., one 45° movement is from DUN→KER then KER→GAL, sharing KER). If the brain region carries information about the concept, the 180° direction would show higher pattern similarity than the other directions whether or not there is an underlying grid-like signal. One hint of evidence supporting a grid-like representation the right EHC is that the pattern dissimilarities appear to increase from “zero” to “small” to “large” changes in the predicted grid-model RDM ( 

Figure 1E

https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2021.620056/full#F1

, right, bar-plot inset). Although the numerical trend matches the 6-fold prediction, it is unclear whether the pattern dissimilarities for “small” and “large” are statistically distinguishable, and the main result could still be driven by the small dissimilarities in the “zero” condition (i.e., 180°). Future work could use a larger set of exemplars and concept labels to test a wider range of movement directions and hence provide further evidence for the emergence of a grid-like representation in concept space after learning.

It is notable that Viganò and Piazza ( 2020 ) did not find distance-based representations in the hippocampus, for either category or sensory spaces. Structures in the MTL have been implicated in a wide range of cognitive functions from spatial navigation to memory to concept formation. We provide a brief overview of these functions and speculate on the possible reasons for the absence of hippocampal involvement in the current study. First, the hippocampus is a region strongly implicated in spatial navigation, where place cells are thought to track an agent's physical location (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978 ). Relatedly, human neuroimaging studies have implicated the hippocampus in tracking distances in virtual spaces (Deuker et al., 2016 ), conceptual spaces (Tavares et al., 2015 ; Theves et al., 2019 , 2020 ) and graph-like relational knowledge structures (Garvert et al., 2017 ). The MTL has long been acknowledged for its role in learning and memory (Nadel and Moscovitch, 1997 ). MTL structures such as the hippocampus, EHC, parahippocampal cortex, and perirhinal cortex are involved in the integration of multiple sources of information such as object identity and spatio-temporal context into a coherent episodic event representation that can be consolidated into memory (Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2008 ; Knierim et al., 2014 ). Interestingly, the role of the MTL in semantic memory has been debated (Squire and Zola-Morgan, 1991 ; Mishkin et al., 1998 ; Duff et al., 2020 ) with some researchers arguing for the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) as the crucial region for representing semantic knowledge, supported by semantic deficits in semantic dementia (Ralph et al., 2016 ). Recent work also showed the involvement of MTL structures such as the hippocampus in concept learning and categorization (Davis et al., 2012 ; Mack et al., 2016 ; Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018 ), with theoretical proposals arguing for an intrinsic link between episodic memory and concept formation (Mack et al., 2018 ). One reason why the hippocampus was not identified in the experiment by Viganò and Piazza ( 2020 ) may be that the new category knowledge had already become consolidated into cortex over the nine days of training, and therefore was no longer hippocampally dependent (Squire et al., 2015 ). Consistent with this, studies that showed hippocampal involvement in concept learning tested participants relatively early in the learning phase (Davis et al., 2012 ; Mack et al., 2016 ). On the other hand, involvement of the EHC in representing conceptual information after long periods of learning as show in Viganò and Piazza's study can inform the debate about the possible role of the MTL structures in organizing semantic knowledge. Future studies could clarify the differential contributions of these MTL structures by tracking neural representations at multiple stages of learning, before and after consolidation.

Another way to uncover the neural representations underlying abstract concepts is to develop computational models that also learn categories (Nosofsky, 1986 ; Kruschke, 1992 ; Nosofsky et al., 1994 ; Ashby et al., 1998 ; Smith and Minda, 1998 ; Love et al., 2004 ; Sanborn et al., 2010 ), and search the brain for representations that match those learned by the models. This approach has focused on the hippocampus (Mack et al., 2016 ; Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018 ) though a recent model based on clustering theories of concept learning was able to capture both hippocampal representations in category learning tasks and place and grid cell-like representations in navigation contexts (Mok and Love, 2019 ). Applied to a concept structure similar to the one in the current study, the model would learn the centers of the concept distributions (representing the category prototypes), and predict stronger activity for category prototypes than non-prototypes, and more similar representations for movements between category prototypes compared to movements toward non-prototype exemplars. This prediction could not be tested in the current study because the exemplars were equally distant from their category prototype. By expanding the sensory space to include more exemplars and testing more movement directions, future studies may be able to distinguish this model from others, by comparing the similarity spaces within brain regions with similarity spaces implied by different computational models (e.g., spatial, clustering, exemplar, Bayesian models).

While brain-imaging studies provide growing evidence for general-purpose neural mechanisms across spatial and conceptual domains, an older line of behavioral work challenges these ideas by showing that people violate axiomatic assumptions in geometric theories of conceptual organization (Tversky and Gati, 1982 ). If conceptual spaces are represented geometrically (Gärdenfors, 2000 ; Bellmund et al., 2018 ), then they must obey several geometric properties, such as the “triangle inequality.” This states that a direct path between two points cannot be larger than an indirect one going through a third point. Using two-dimensional stimuli similar to ones used in neuroimaging studies (e.g., Constantinescu et al., 2016 ), Tversky and Gati ( 1982 ) showed that people's judgments of the dissimilarity between pairs of exemplars imply internal conceptual spaces that violate the triangle inequality. While augmented geometric models have been developed to address this problem (Krumhansl, 1978 ; Nosofsky, 1991 ), some theoretical issues remain (Goldstone and Son, 2012 ). Therefore, proposals that suggest that spatial representations underlie human concept learning need to address this challenge to resolve the tension between neural data and human behavioral data.

In summary, Viganò and Piazza ( 2020 ) provide an important contribution to the growing evidence for shared neural mechanisms underlying spatial navigation and abstract knowledge. Future paradigms should further disentangle the contributions of the hippocampus, the EHC, and the mPFC to the representation of category vs. sensory spaces, assess learning and consolidation-dependent changes in neural representations, and compare computational models in their ability to match neural and behavioral data. Together, these developments will clarify the extent to which we can generalize mechanistic insights from spatial navigation to the organization of higher-order knowledge structures.

### FUENTE: MemoRAG: Memory-Augmented RAG - Emergent Mind ###
### TIPO: web_page | URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/memorag | CARACTERES: 15913 ###
### KEYWORDS: Dual-system architecture, Global memory compression, Clue-guided retrieval, KV compression techniques, Long-context processing ###

Resumen: This article introduces **MemoRAG**, an advanced technical framework designed to overcome the limitations of standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation when dealing with **long-context datasets** and ambiguous user queries. The text details a unique **dual-system architecture** that utilizes a lightweight memory model to condense massive amounts of information through **global memory compression** and a more powerful generator model to produce accurate answers. By generating intermediate **clue-guided retrieval** hints, the system effectively bridges the gap between vague questions and scattered evidence across a vast knowledge base. Ultimately, the source highlights how this approach achieves **superior efficiency and accuracy** compared to traditional methods, enabling AI to process up to one million tokens while reducing computational costs.

MemoRAG: Memory-Augmented RAG

Updated 31 October 2025

MemoRAG is a memory-augmented RAG framework that integrates global memory compression with clue-guided retrieval to process long, complex contexts.

Its dual-system architecture features a lightweight memory model for semantic summarization and an expressive generator model for detailed answer synthesis.

Empirical evaluations show MemoRAG improves retrieval accuracy and efficiency on benchmark long-context tasks compared to traditional RAG systems.

MemoRAG is a memory-augmented 

Retrieval-Augmented Generation

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/retrieval-augmented-generation-rag

 ( 

RAG

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/multi-turn-retrieval-augmented-generation-rag

) framework designed to address the computational and conceptual challenges inherent in processing long contexts with LLMs. Unlike conventional approaches, MemoRAG utilizes a 

dual-system architecture

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/dual-system-architecture

 that integrates global memory compression and clue-guided retrieval to improve both the efficiency and efficacy of knowledge-intensive LLM tasks.

1. Motivation and Limitations of Conventional RAG

Traditional RAG systems equip LLMs to answer questions by providing external, retrieved knowledge documents as additional context. These systems excel when queries are explicit and the underlying knowledge source is well-structured, but exhibit marked limitations when facing:

Ambiguous information needs (implicit, underspecified, or indirect queries).

Unstructured and distributed knowledge (evidence scattered across large or poorly indexed corpora).

Complex aggregation tasks (requiring synthesis of information from varied, distant contexts).

LLMs, even those with extended context windows (32K–128K tokens), encounter escalating computational costs and limited performance in such long-context scenarios. Classic RAG frameworks generally require precisely formulated queries and pre-organized knowledge, constraints that do not generalize to real-world, complex applications ( 

Qian et al., 2024

https://www.emergentmind.com/papers/2409.05591

).

2. Dual-System Architecture of MemoRAG

MemoRAG adopts a dual-system design inspired by cognitive models of human memory (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968):

Light, Long-Range System (Memory Model):

 Operates as a global memory builder, processing the entire available database to construct a compressed global memory representation. This system is lightweight (cost-efficient), length-agnostic (able to handle up to millions of tokens), and optimized for capturing broad semantic context.

Expensive, Expressive System (Generator Model):

 This 

generative LLM

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/generative-llm-gemini-2-0-flash

 leverages clues and retrieved evidence from the memory model to synthesize the final answer. It is computationally demanding but necessary for high-fidelity language generation.

Workflow:

The memory model first encodes all input text into global memory using KV compression techniques.

Upon receiving a task, the memory model produces clues (draft answers or retrieval hints) tailored to guide downstream retrieval.

Clues are used to locate pertinent evidence from the long context.

The generator consumes the query and retrieved evidence to generate the final output.

3. Global Memory Compression: Technical Constructs

MemoRAG realizes its memory mechanism via 

KV compression

, whereby raw input tokens are mapped to a compact set of memory tokens. This not only reduces the number of tokens to be attended over, but also facilitates semantic abstraction.

KV Compression Attention Formula

For a sequence of tokens { x 1 , ... , x n } {x_1, ..., x_n} { x 1 ,..., x n } processed by transformer model Θ ( ⋅ ) \Theta(\cdot) Θ( ⋅) with context window l l l compressed into k k k ( k ≪ l k \ll l k ≪ l) memory tokens:

Q m = X m W Q m Q^m = X^m W_Q^m Q m= X m W Q m , K m = X m W K m K^m = X^m W_K^m K m= X m W K m , V m = X m W V m V^m = X^m W_V^m V m= X m W V m  are the projections for memory tokens.

Memory attention is computed:

Attention ( Q , K , V ) = softmax ( [ Q ; Q m ] [ K ; K m ; K cache m ] T d k ) [ V , V m , V cache m ] \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax} \left(\frac{[Q; Q^m] [K; K^m; K^m_{\text{cache}}]^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) [V, V^m, V^m_{\text{cache}}] Attention( Q, K, V)= softmax( d k  [ Q; Q m][ K; K m; K cache m ] T )[ V, V m, V cache m ]

where K cache m K^m_{\text{cache}} K cache m  and V cache m V^m_{\text{cache}} V cache m  serve to retain memory state across window boundaries.

A critical operation is the periodic discarding of raw token caches after compression, mimicking a "forgetting" process. After processing n n n windows, the original context is reduced to n × k n \times k n × k memory tokens.

4. Clue-Guided Retrieval and Feedback Reinforcement

MemoRAG introduces staged clue generation—whereby the memory model, upon receiving a query q q q and (compressed) context c c c, generates a set of clues y y y that narrow the semantic gap between query and answer-bearing evidence. The generator Θ \Theta Θ then utilizes these clues to 

retrieve

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/jetson-nano-r-retrieve

 c ^ \hat{c} c^ and produce the final answer a a a:

a = Θ ( q , c ^ ∣ θ ) a = \Theta(q, \hat{c} \mid \theta) a= Θ( q, c^ ∣ θ)

c ^ = Γ ( y , c ∣ γ ) \hat{c} = \Gamma(y, c \mid \gamma) c^= Γ( y, c ∣ γ)

y = Θ mem ( q , c ∣ θ mem ) y = \Theta_{\text{mem}}(q, c \mid \theta_{\text{mem}}) y= Θ mem ( q, c ∣ θ mem )

Training incorporates 

Reinforcement Learning

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/reinforcement-learning-q-learning

 by Generation quality's Feedback (RLGF): feedback from generation quality is used to optimize the ability of the memory model to produce clues that maximize downstream retrieval and answer accuracy.

5. Experimental Evaluation

MemoRAG is validated on a comprehensive suite of long-context and standard tasks:

Benchmarks:

 NarrativeQA, Qasper, MultiFieldQA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMQA, GovReport, MultiNews, En.SUM, ∞ \infty ∞ Bench, and 

UltraDomain

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/ultradomain

 (datasets with up to 1M tokens per sample).

Baseline comparisons:

 Standard RAG variants (dense/sparse retrieval), full-context LLMs (no retrieval), query rewriting (RQ-RAG), synthetic document generation (HyDE).

Findings:

On UltraDomain and other long-context tasks, MemoRAG outperforms all RAG and full-context baselines (highest F1 scores for in-domain and out-of-domain queries).

MemoRAG distinctly excels at bridging distributed evidence and ambiguous queries, outperforming models limited by context window or static retrieval approaches.

On standard QA and summarization, MemoRAG yields better retrieval, aggregation, and coherence compared to both classical methods and full-context transformers.

The architecture generalizes well across domains, showing adaptability to different types of knowledge and tasks.

6. Efficiency, Generalization, and Future Directions

MemoRAG's memory model is lightweight and length-efficient, permitting deployment at scale (GPUs from T4 to A100; up to 1M tokens). The dual-system design means only the global memory and clue sets—not the full context—are attended during expensive answer generation, lowering inference and storage costs compared to context-heavy transformer variants.

MemoRAG is robust to scaling: it generalizes to longer contexts than trained for, mitigates the "lost-in-the-middle" effect, and efficiently aggregates evidence for complex synthesis tasks. A plausible implication is that these architectural advantages open new areas for memory-augmented conversational agents, information aggregation systems, and personalized assistants where memory, scaling, and accuracy are critical.

7. Key Formula and Summary Table

MemoRAG Pipeline: a = Θ ( q , c ^ ∣ θ ) c ^ = Γ ( y , c ∣ γ ) y = Θ mem ( q , c ∣ θ mem ) \boxed{ a = \Theta(q, \hat{c} \mid \theta) \ \hat{c} = \Gamma(y, c \mid \gamma) \ y = \Theta_{\text{mem}}(q, c \mid \theta_{\text{mem}}) } a= Θ( q, c^ ∣ θ) c^= Γ( y, c ∣ γ) y= Θ mem ( q, c ∣ θ mem )

8. Conclusion

MemoRAG represents a methodologically distinct, memory-inspired 

retrieval augmentation

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/retrieval-augmentation

 framework for LLMs. It leverages efficient memory compression, clue-guided retrieval, and feedback reinforcement to address the limitations of context length, unstructured knowledge, and complex aggregation in traditional RAG systems. Its state-of-the-art empirical performance and scalability indicate that 

memory augmentation

https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/memory-augmentation

 is a necessary advancement for robust, long-context processing in modern LLMs ( 

Qian et al., 2024

https://www.emergentmind.com/papers/2409.05591

).

### FUENTE: Methods For Ad Hoc And Conversational Entity Retrieval From Knowledge Graphs - Digital Commons @ Wayne State ###
### TIPO: pdf | URL: https://digitalcommons.wayne.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4549&context=oa_dissertations | CARACTERES: 184878 ###
### KEYWORDS: Entity Retrieval Methods, Knowledge Graph Embeddings, Sequential Dependence Models, Conversational Search Systems, Structured Data Retrieval ###

Resumen: This research paper introduces two advanced models, **PFSDM and PFFDM**, designed to improve how search engines find specific information within complex **knowledge graphs**. Unlike traditional methods that treat every part of a query with equal importance, these new frameworks use **statistical and linguistic features** to dynamically map individual keywords or phrases to the most relevant fields of an entity, such as its name, category, or attributes. By accounting for **sequential and full term dependencies**, the models can more accurately interpret the intent behind natural language questions and "telegraphic" keyword searches. Experimental results on datasets like **DBpedia** demonstrate that this flexible, **feature-based projection** significantly outperforms existing retrieval models, particularly when handling descriptive or complex user inquiries.

CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION 

According to the studies [90, 61, 115], 71% of queries issued to the Web search engines 

include named entities, while the intent of nearly 75% of queries is to find information 

about entities (such as people, organizations, locations, scientific papers, products, etc.). 

The information needs of users issuing such queries are better addressed when results are 

presented as a list of relevant entities or an information box about the entity of interest that 

presents a user with a piece of summary information on the entity, compared to presenting 

the user with full documents that merely mention the entities and placing the burden of 

locating and finding the necessary information about them on the user. 

Progress in the development of online collaborative knowledge editing and informa-

tion extraction methods lead to the emergence of large-scale knowledge repositories, such 

as YAGO1, DBpedia2, and Wikidata3 which adopt a subject-predicate-object triple-based 

data model. A subject in those triples designates an entity, which could be either physi-

cal or abstract (e.g. person, location, book, organization, conference, color, mathematical 

concept, species, etc.). An object is either another entity or a textual literal, while pred-

icate corresponds to the kind of a relationship between the subject and object entities 

(e.g. 

marriedTo, starredIn, treatsDisease, isCeoOf 

etc.). Therefore, the knowledge stored 

in these repositories conceptually forms a large directed labeled multi-graph (i.e. knowl-

edge graph) with nodes corresponding to entities and edges denoting typed relationships. 

Furthermore, YAGO, DBpedia, and Wikidata are not standalone knowledge graphs. More 

and more Web sources join the Linked Open Data (LOD) movement4 and make publicly 

1http://yago-knowledge.org 2http://dbpedia.org 3http://wikidata.org 4https://www.w3.org/wiki/LinkedData

2 available structured and linked data records in the form of the triples in the Resource De-

scription Framework5 (RDF) format along with the more traditional for the Web textual 

human-readable form. In the RDF framework, entities are identified using the Uniform 

Resource Identifiers (URIs), which are URL-based. URIs allow to look up (dereference) 

structured information about each entity on-line. URIs also allow linking entities in differ-

ent knowledge bases that describe the same real-world entity (e.g. an entity in DBpedia 

that describes the same entity as an entity in Wikidata). Cross-linked knowledge bases 

form the Web of Linked Data [68] or the Linked Open Data cloud6, a giant distributed 

knowledge graph. As of May 2020, the Web of Data consisted of 1301 datasets, which in-

cluded over 413 billion RDF triples of semi-structured data from heterogeneous interlinked 

domains, from media and geography to linguistics and life sciences. 

The scale and richness of knowledge stored in the Linked Data knowledge graphs, as 

well as its structure, makes it a natural choice for addressing (or helping to address) a 

variety of entity-centric information needs formulated as keyword queries and gives rise 

to the task of ad hoc entity retrieval from graphs (ERKG), which we are interested in 

studying. This task is fundamentally different from traditional ad hoc or Web IR setting 

since it considers entities (or structured entity representations) in knowledge graph as 

units of retrieval. It is also quite different from both ad hoc entity retrieval [7], where the 

task is to retrieve named entities embedded in documents, and using knowledge bases to 

improve document retrieval [83, 150, 149, 39, 129, 128]. 

A closely related task is an entity retrieval from knowledge graphs, performed in a 

5http://www.w3.org/RDF 6http://lod-cloud.net

3 conversational setting. Here, the user asks the system a series of questions and expects to 

receive an entity from a knowledge graph as an answer. This problem can be alternatively 

formulated as a sequential simple question answering over a knowledge graph. 

ERKG is a challenging problem, since the structure of knowledge graphs is tradition-

ally optimized for executing structured queries that use logical operations and performing 

automated reasoning, but is not conducive to answering “telegraphic” keyword queries 

common in Web search. Entity retrieval from knowledge graph requires accurate under-

standing and semantic matching of unstructured textual queries with graph-based entity 

representations. Query understanding in this context involves not only accounting for po-

tential dependencies between the query terms and determining the relative importance of 

concepts contained in a query for conveying the information need underlying the query 

but also accurately projecting query segments onto structured entity representations. Se-

mantic matching is needed in order to overcome the vocabulary mismatch, which in the 

case of ERKG, requires retrieval models to be aware of semantic relationships between 

entity attributes and categories, in addition to the ones between individual words. In the 

dialog setting, there also arises a need to determine the relevance of entities in the current 

conversational context. 

None of the existing IR or database techniques satisfies all of the necessary require-

ments listed above to be successfully applied to the task of ERKG. In particular, structured 

query languages for triple stores, such as SPARQL, are based only on 

syntactic matching 

of graph patterns 

and thus are suitable only for a limited number of information access 

patterns. Unranked results of exact matching of queries expressed in SPARQL language 

are also incapable to properly satisfy the users’ information needs by returning either too

4 few or too many result hits. In addition to that, to be properly utilized, these query lan-

guages require the knowledge of schema of a given knowledge base and technical skills 

required to properly formulate a query, which many end-users typically do not possess. 

Existing models for structured document retrieval, such as the Mixture of Language Mod-

els (MLM) [110], BM25F [122] and Probabilistic Retrieval Model for Semistructured Data 

(PRMS) [79] assume the bag-of-words representations of queries and documents (and thus 

do not account for dependencies between the query terms) and thus are incapable of differ-

entiating the relative importance of query concepts represented as terms and phrases. On 

the other hand, retrieval models that incorporate term dependencies [96] and estimate 

the importance of query terms or phrases [13] do not take into the account document 

structure. 

Models for retrieving entities from knowledge graphs play an important role in many 

information seeking scenarios: 

1. They can be used for implementing search systems that would allow users to pose 

complex keyword queries to obtain and interact with structured knowledge in the Web 

of Data. Keyword-based search tools of this kind do not require users to master query 

languages or know the underlying schema of a knowledge repository to be able to work 

with it. 

2. They can be used for obtaining more accurate and complete initial results for com-

plex entity-centric information needs than existing retrieval models. These results can 

be consecutively expanded or re-ranked by the task-specific approaches. Alternatively, 

ERKG models can pick entities of user’s interest as the starting point for further explo-

5 ration of user’s information needs. 

3. They can be used for supplementing the search results that are obtained with document-

based retrieval models (such as Web search results) with entity-focused structured 

knowledge for the same keyword query [59]. 

4. They can be used to improve the completeness and accuracy of results for document 

retrieval. 

Despite their wide applicability, models for ad hoc and conversational entity retrieval 

from knowledge graphs have received little research attention. Entity retrieval from knowl-

edge graphs is an important part of the methods for entity linking [97, 101, 85, 63, 18, 56], 

recommendation [87] and interactive knowledge base exploration [99] and, therefore, 

they can all benefit from the proposed retrieval models. 

The shift from retrieval from the Web of documents to retrieval from the Web of entities, 

however, raises many research questions, including: (1) which representation method 

for entities is the most effective in capturing their semantics; (2) how to map terms and 

phrases in unstructured keyword queries onto structured entity representations; (3) how 

to effectively utilize dialog context when entity retrieval is performed in a conversational 

setting.

6 

CHAPTER 2 RELATED WORK 

2.1 Ad hoc Entity Retrieval Task 

The general task of ad-hoc object retrieval from the Web of Data was first defined by 

Pound et al. [115] as “answering arbitrary information needs related to particular aspects 

of objects (entities) expressed in unconstrained natural language and resolved using a 

collection of structured data (such as a knowledge graph)”. Based on a large-scale analysis 

of Web search logs, they classified information needs related to the task of ERKG into the 

ones that aim at finding specific entities (e.g. “cj5 jeep”), type queries aiming at finding 

entities sharing a particular attribute (e.g. “formula 1 drivers who won the monaco grand 

prix”), attribute queries (e.g. “zip code waterville maine”) and relation queries that aim 

at finding how two or more entities or types are related (“who is tom cruise married to”). 

However, they did not propose any retrieval models to address this task. Many commercial 

search engines provide entity retrival functionality for simple queries (see Figure 1), but 

often fail to retrieve related entities on more complex queries (see Figure 2). 

Previously proposed methods focused on addressing each of those information needs 

individually and typically involve a pre-processing step, during which an entity document 

(profile) is constructed for each entity by aggregating all the triples that include the entity 

URI. These predicates are grouped into fields of structured entity representations by type 

[112], according to manually determined importance [16], using a fixed scheme with a 

fixed number of fields (e.g. title and content [105] or entity name, attributes, categories, 

similar and related entity names [163]) or a two-level hierarchy, in which the first level 

corresponds to predicate types and the the second level corresponds to individual pred-

icates [104]. The entity retrieval process adopted by these methods typically consists of

https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/notebooklm/AKXwDQHMnV3ytIPlrijFY9mVD8WhnDndTGozf7ulfiESe-ugfGhJm-uJOMe28xgJpZv6VwJdaRQP28rJ8zZavNQ8zuz1mrGiP6fWpl7kaKMDdBnLlNOixMYd1BhyEgeTK0CPkA5ZKWng=w1198-h476-v0

f39ac199-30c9-41a7-a784-e9fc983c7c99

7 Figure 1: Commercial search engine results for the query “presidents of the united states”. 

Figure 2: Commercial search engine results for the query “Neil Gaiman novels adapted to film”. Relevant results are highlighted in green.

8 two stages. A set of entities retrieved for a keyword query or question in the first stage 

is expanded with immediate neighbors obtained using spreading activation, random walk, 

or SPARQL queries in the second stage. Despite the importance of accurate results for the 

initial entity retrieval in the first stage to the overall success of these methods, due to the 

lack of better alternatives, they utilized standard retrieval models, such as BM25 [137], 

BM25F [16, 17, 54, 137], Kullback-Leibler divergence [6, 7, 56] or the Mixture of Lan-

guage Models (MLM) [25, 104, 108, 162], which do not account for the implicit structure 

of entity-centric queries as well as the dependencies and proximity of query terms. 

Specifically, Tonon et al. [137] proposed a hybrid method combining IR and struc-

tured graph search that starts by retrieving an initial set of entities from an inverted index 

of multi-fielded entity documents by using BM25 retrieval model and then extends it with 

the entities that are attached to the ones in the initial search results with certain predicates, 

such as owl:sameAs, dbpedia:wikilink, dbpedia:disambiguates and dbpedia:redirect. 

Since the related entities are found by exploiting specific datatype properties, their ap-

proach is only applicable to entity retrieval from a subset of the Web of Data centered 

around DBpedia. It also uses a Jaro-Winkler similarity metric, which calculates the match-

ing based on the original textual representation of entities and hence does not solve the 

issue of vocabulary mismatch. A generalized approach based on spreading activation on se-

mantic graphs for expansion of the initial set of entities obtained with any retrieval model 

was proposed in [123]. A learning-to-rank method for re-ranking the results of MLM using 

query term and structural entity similarity features has been proposed in [162]. Bron et 

al. [25] proposed a method for entity list completion that combined entity representations 

as structured documents based on the incoming and outgoing links to/from other entities

9 and also used the MLM as a retrieval model. 

The SemSets method [32] proposed for entity list search utilizes the relevance of enti-

ties to automatically constructed categories or semantic sets measured using structural and 

textual similarity. Their approach combines a retrieval model (they used a simple TF-IDF-

based retrieval model) with the ranking based on propagating activation over the knowl-

edge graph’s link structure and evaluation of membership in semantic sets. Sawant and 

Chakrabarti [125] proposed a learning-to-rank method for handling Web queries aimed at 

finding entities of a specific type. He and Xin [67] proposed a method for expanding a 

seed set of entities into a larger set of semantically related entities. 

Several proposed approaches to question answering over linked data are based on 

translation of natural language questions into structured SPARQL queries [139, 130, 152]. 

These approaches, however, do not consider term dependencies and are based on syntactic 

matching of SPARQL queries and thus may suffer from vocabulary mismatch. 

Other related work focused on entity-related retrieval scenarios that are conceptually 

different from the task of ERKG. Elbassuoni and Blanco [49] proposed a method for key-

word search over RDF graphs that represents subject-predicate-object triples as documents 

and returns a sorted list of RDF subgraphs constructed by joining the triples retrieved by 

using each individual query term. Guo et al. [61] proposed a probabilistic language 

model learned through weak supervision that learns to associate lyrics with music and 

address with organization. Herzig and Tran [69] proposed a method for querying multi-

ple heterogeneous Web data repositories using structured SPARQL queries that constructs 

on-the-fly mappings between entity attributes. First, they construct a language model for 

each distinct entity attribute from the descriptions of the top retrieved entities by issuing

10 

an original query to one of the repositories and then determine the mappings between 

entity attributes across repositories by calculating the negative cross-entropy between the 

language models of those attributes. Cheng et al. [29] and Nie et al. [108] proposed 

a language modeling-based methods based on MLM for retrieval of Web objects, which 

are aggregate units of information about people, products, papers, locations, and orga-

nizations extracted from different Web sources. Lin et al. [90] proposed an automatic 

approach to identify relevant actions for Web search queries that are actionable. For exam-

ple for a query “sea world location” a relevant action would be to show the exact address 

and a map. 

Before knowledge graphs became widespread and popular, several evaluation cam-

paigns conducted by TREC and INEX focused on the tasks related to entity retrieval 

from 

documents. 

The goals of these tasks varied from retrieving Wikipedia articles about entities 

that match keyword queries to finding named entities mentioned in Web pages or textual 

documents. In particular, the Entity track at TREC [8, 10] provided two search tasks: re-

lated entity finding and entity list completion. The goal of the related entity ranking task 

[24, 92] is to find and rank the related entities given a structured query that specifies an 

input entity, the type of the relevant entities, and the relationship between the input and 

relevant entities in the context of a given textual collection. Expert finding [5] is a special 

case of the related entity finding problem in the context of enterprise search, which is fo-

cused on specific input entities (e.g. expertise area) and particular types of related entities 

(e.g. employee) and relations (e.g. expert in). The goal of the entity list completion task is 

to retrieve entities with common properties given example entities. INEX Entity Ranking 

track (INEX-XER) [40, 43, 45] provided similar tasks, which were, however, focused more

11 

on the type of target entities than on the relation between the target and input entities. In 

the entity ranking task, the goal was to return a ranked list of entities, where each entity 

has an associated Wikipedia page and a set of categories specifying the entity’s type, given 

a topic consisting of the keyword query as well as a set of example entities and target 

entity category. Due to the narrow focus of this task, all methods proposed to address it 

[6, 7, 77, 76, 44], besides the text of Wikipedia articles, also leveraged diverse meta-data 

associated with them, such as category and disambiguation information along with the 

link structure. 

It was also previously shown that entities associated with an information need under-

lying a query can be leveraged to improve the results of document retrieval for the same 

query. Sayyadian et al. [126] found out that selective utilization of structured information 

from relational databases for expansion of entity-centric keyword queries (e.g. aimed at 

finding a researcher in a bibliographic database) improves their accuracy. Schuhmacher et 

al. [128] proposed a method for ranking the mentions of entities that are extracted from 

the top documents returned for a keyword query using four types of features: (1) mention, 

(2) query-mention, (3) query-entity, and (4) entity-entity features. 

Methods for graph database search using structured queries [153] as well as keyword-

based search in relational and XML databases have been proposed and studied by the 

database community. However, such settings are also quite different from entity retrieval 

from knowledge graphs, since keyword-based search over relational and general data 

graphs typically returns a list of non-redundant Steiner trees [2, 75, 15, 91, 1, 71, 55] 

or sub-graphs [89] sorted by their relevance calculated by counting the occurrences of 

query terms. Result ranking models in graph database search typically leverage the struc-

12 

ture of results by node and edge weights aggregation [1] , attribute-value statistics in both 

the database and the workload [27] or a combination of these properties with information 

retrieval content-based relevance measures, such as TF-IDF weighting [33, 29, 71, 89], 

probabilistic [27] or language models [108], and term proximity [55]. Elbassuoni et al. 

[50] proposed a method for ranking the results of structured queries that consist of triple 

patterns over RDF repositories using language modeling. The method first constructs lan-

guage models (LMs) for both the queries and each possible result subgraph and then ranks 

the subgraphs using the Kullback-Leibler divergence between their LMs and the query LM. 

2.2 Fielded Retrieval Models 

Efficient way to improve effectiveness of retrieval that can be applied to most collec-

tions as well as for ERKG [163], is to apply more detailed view to textual documents and 

consider them as having multiple pre-defined fields instead of usual case of considering 

them as unstructured free-text data. For example, for scientific collections we can consider 

paper as just a piece of unstructured text, or take into account paper structure and work 

with different parts of it such as title, abstract, paper body in different way. Intuitively, 

second approach that consider title and abstract as having higher “importance” should 

achieve higher performance then former apporach as papers are more likely to have men-

tions of their key concepts in titles and abstracts, and users are usually perform searches 

by using these key concepts in their queries. 

Usually in IR this apporch is implemented by modification of various state-of-the-art 

non-fielded models. There are different ways to do this, though. First aspect in which mod-

els differ is how to transform matching score formula for query and document f(Q,D) into 

f(Q,D1, . . . , DF ) where D1...F are document fields. For language modelling based models

13 

this usually is achieved by mixing language models for all document fields as described 

in [110]. For models that are not directly based on language modelling this can be eas-

ily achived by representing f(Q,D1, . . . , DF ) = ∑ j 

wjf(Q,Dj) where f(Q,Dj) is the same 

scoring function as for non-fielded document applied to j-th document field and wj is rel-

ative importance of j-th field. However, as was shown in [160] the better approach is to 

preserve nonlinearity of f(Q,D) and perform combination of fields inside it. This approach 

is more simple, requires less parameters to tune and usually yields higher performance. 

The idea of utilizing document’s fields has it roots in the research directions of meta-

search [4] and XML retrieval [57]. XML and SGML documents usually have complicated 

structure, and it was observed that focusing on individual fields usually formed from con-

tent of particular tags, is helpful to effectively and efficiently exploit document structure 

[147]. Combining scores from individual document fields into one final score can in turn 

be seen as a meta-search problem where fields are treated as different representations of 

a document [110, 36]. 

In the [110] authors build a connection between areas of meta-search and combining 

document representations (fields) by checking whether three meta-search hypothesis hold 

for combining document representations. Namely, they check whether (1) compatibility of 

outputs (2) good quality of each individual representation (3) lower variance of ranks for 

relevant documents than for ranks for non-relevant documents is neccessary for successful 

combination of document representations for the task of known-item search, when only 

one document is relevant to a query. They conclude that unlike for meta-search only 

(1) is neccessary for combining representations. Another contribution of the paper is the 

development of mixture-based language model (MLM). Authors compare MLM to other

14 

meta-search fusion algorithms applied for the combination of representations and find out 

that MLM significantly outperforms other methods. 

Study [122] in the similar vein proposes term frequency combination as a simple al-

ternative to score combination for multiple fields. In the context of BM25 model authors 

analyze the details of modifications that are necessary with the proposed scheme, for ex-

ample how the increased number of parameters should be tuned. One of the conclusions 

they come to is that it is not always the case that document structure does constitute a 

source of information for relevance, and often it can constitute a distraction instead of an 

improvement. Improved model from [122] is proposed as BM25F model in [160]. The 

most important difference is that each field has separate B parameter. 

One particular direction of work by Jim Young Kim et al. [79, 78] is focused on the 

idea that each term in a query has different field relevance (which is a generalization of 

field weights). In Probabilistic Retrieval Model for Semistructured Data (PRMS) [79] field 

weights for each term are assumed to be equal to posterior mapping probability calcu-

lated with Bayes’ theorem. This simple assumption was lifted in a Field Relevance Model 

(FRM) in favor of the more elaborated approach that uses several sources of field rele-

vance estimation that it mixes together as linear combination where weights are learned 

from training queries. Authors use three sources of estimation: (1) Collection Language 

Model, which were used in the PRMS model (2) Top-k Retrieved Documents, based on 

pseudo relevance feedback (3) Per-Field Weights based on Training Queries, which does 

not depend on query term as in [110, 122]

15 

2.3 Term Dependencies for Information Retrieval 

Term Dependencies are another way to imporve retrieval effectiveness by incorporating 

information about depencencies of terms in user queries and documents. 

In [96] Metzler and Croft propose three ranking models based on Markov Random 

Fields that capture dependencies between query terms in various ways so that they can 

abstract the notions of dependence and co-occurrence. The main contributions of the pa-

pers are: (1) formulation of Full Independence (FIM), Seqential Dependence (SDM), and 

Full Dependence (FDM) models, which are represented by different undirected graphical 

models (see Figure 3), and (2) proposal of a feasible way to train such models by directly 

optimizing mean average precision. Authors use language modelling for estimating fea-

ture values over graph cliques and with this approach Full Independence model reduces to 

the language modeling approach to information retrieval, Sequential Dependence variant 

adds modelling dependencies between adjacent query terms to it, and Full Dependence 

variant attempts to model dependendies between every subset of query terms. Both SDM 

and FDM variant use features for ordered and unordered matches of query n-grams within 

a document. The training method in use optimized three parameters of model (λT,O,U) 

using coordinate ascent method. Results obtained shows that both SDM and FDM improve 

mean average precision, and ordered features are more important for small, homogenous 

newswire collections, while unordered matches are more appropriate for big and noisy 

web collections. 

A weighted variant of the Sequential Dependence model is introduced in [13] as a 

Weighted Sequential Dependence Model (WSDM) which is the first model which takes 

into account term dependencies simultaneously with weighting generic query term con-

Figure 3: Markov random field model variants. D is a document node, and qi are query term nodes. 

cepts in a unified framework. The weights that are assined to concepts are assumed to be 

equal to linear combination of features with particular weights that are learned in a same 

way λ-parameters were learned in [96]. Authors equip both endogenous (based on collec-

tion statistics) and exogenous (based on external resources) features to estimate concept 

weights and perform detailed analysis of a usefullness of them in different scenarios. Also, 

they analyse relative usefullness of weighting for unigram and bigram concepts. They 

found out that in general it is better to use features of both types as well as weighting for 

both unigram and bigram concepts, although there are exceptions to this: for example, for 

short navigational web queries, using only bigram concepts weighting could be beneficial 

to retrieval effectiveness. 

Parameterized Query Expansion (PQE) [14] model generalizes several concept weight-

ing and query expansion approaches. It weights the concept in the same way as in 

Weighted Dependence Model, but in addition to concepts that present in the query itself, 

PQE also uses latent concepts associated with the information need underlying the query 

and obtained through the process of pseudo-relevance feedback. Authors note that PQE

17 

outperforms both previously proposed non-parameterized and parameterized expansion 

methods and is particularly beneficial for verbose natural language queries, while being 

highly effective for short keyword queries too. They observe that PQE can use less number 

of expansion concepts then non-parameterized models while still being more effective, and 

thus keeping query latency lower. 

Query representation used in [96, 13, 14] is advanced one step further with hyper-

graph structure [12]. Instead of modeling dependencies between individual query terms, 

hypergraph structure models dependencies between query concepts such as n-grams, term 

proximities, noun phrases, and phrase entities. While hypergraphs in general are defined 

as a generalization of a graph, where edges can connect more than two vertices, authors 

construct a particular hypergraph for retrieval needs, that includes regular edges between 

concepts and document vertices (local hyperedges) that model the contribution of concepts 

to document relevance in the same way as in [96, 13, 14] as well as global hyperedge over 

all of the query concepts. Global hyperedge provides the evidence about the contribution 

of each query concept to document relevance given its dependency on the entire set of 

query concepts. Based on the observation that the co-occurrence of concepts in one pas-

sage of text is a strong indicator of their dependency, authors use approach from Max-Psg 

retrieval model to calculate concepts interdependence by using the passage of a document 

with the highest score. Results obtained indicate a certain overlap between the effect of 

term dependencies (concepts) and higher-order term dependencies (global hyperedge) on 

retrieval effectiveness.

18 

2.4 Word Embeddings in Information Retrieval 

Significant research efforts in the IR community were devoted to assessing the utility of 

word embeddings for different IR tasks. While the initial and some of the recent works in 

this area directly utilize word embeddings obtained using the methods such as word2vec, 

several word embedding models specifically targeting IR [46, 159, 120] have been recently 

proposed. The Dual Embedding Space Model [102] utilizes embedding matrices, which 

correspond to the two layers of the CBOW or Skip-gram architectures, to re-rank retrieval 

results. Experiments with this model indicate that utilizing IN-OUT instead of IN-IN simi-

larity between embeddings of a query and document words allows for better modeling of 

aboutness 

of a document with respect to a query. 

2.5 Network Embeddings 

Network embedding models aim to embed network nodes into a low-dimensional vec-

tor space. A common idea underlying these methods is the adoption of the embedding 

methods from language modeling to sequences obtained using random walks on a given 

network. DeepWalk [113] is the first method that is based on this idea. DeepWalk trains 

the Skip-Gram architecture on sequences of vertices generated by random walks of speci-

fied length starting from each node in the network. The resulting embeddings can be used 

for various classification tasks, such as group labeling in social networks. Other notable 

network embedding methods are LINE [136], node2vec [58], and struc2vec [121]. 

2.6 Knowledge Graph Embeddings 

Knowledge graph embeddings are a popular way to obtain low-dimensional dense rep-

resentations for entities and predicates. A widely known TransE model [21] was pro-

posed as a way to greatly reduce the number of parameters required to train the Struc-

19 

tured Embeddings model [22] by using vector algebra. MEmbER [73] is an extension 

of GloVe [111] to learn conceptual spaces consisting of word and entity embeddings, in 

which the salient words in a given domain are associated with separating hyperplanes. 

Several studies [143, 148, 164] proposed a hybrid between entity and word embeddings 

by employing a loss function, which includes both a TransE-based component to model 

relations between entities and a word2vec-based component to model semantic relations 

between the words along with the third component, whose purpose is to align entity and 

word embeddings obtained by the first two components. In [106] authors take a different 

approach by learning word and entity embeddings without utilizing relations between en-

tities from a knowledge graph and instead relying only on an unannotated corpus of text. 

None of the previously proposed approaches for learning joint word and entity embedding 

spaces were proposed specifically for entity search in a knowledge graph, and thus ignore 

important information, such as knowledge graph structural components. 

2.7 Simple Question Answering over KG 

Simple questions are factoid questions, for which the answer is a single KG entity in 

the object position of a KG triple representing a simple fact about another entity. The 

nature of these questions allows to automatically construct large-scale datasets to train 

neural architectures for simple QA [20]. The methods previously proposed for simple QA 

can be grouped into two categories: end-to-end neural networks [95, 66] and pipelined 

approaches [155, 138, 103, 94]. End-to-end neural networks typically consist of the layers 

that obtain question and triple embeddings and the layer(s) that compute(s) the matching 

score between the triple and question embeddings. Pipelined approaches +proposed for 

this task include entity linking and predicate classification implemented as CNNs [155],

20 

RNNs [138, 103], their modifications [103, 114] or transformers [94]. 

2.8 Memory Networks for QA 

Memory networks (MemNNs) [146] are a class of differentiable models, which can 

perform simple inference over structured and unstructured knowledge. In MemNNs, a 

controller neural network performs inference steps (hops) over memories. The first hop 

combines embeddings of the original query and the memory cell most similar to it, with 

each subsequent hop adding more matching memories. MemNNs were shown to perform 

well in goal-oriented [19] and non-goal-oriented [47] dialog systems as well as in factual 

reasoning and deduction for story-based QA [145, 70]. Key-value MemNNs [100], in 

which the memories are indexed by keys, were shown to be effective at retrieving answers 

in text-based QA and integration of task-oriented dialog systems with knowledge bases 

[52]. 

2.9 Graph Convolutional Neural Networks 

Propagation of information between graph nodes in neural models is utilized in Graph 

Convolutional Networks (GCNs) [42, 81] and their variants, such as R-GCN [127], Graph-

SAGE [62] and GAT [140]. However, GCNs are focused on graph node representation 

learning and not on relevance computation. 

2.10 Conversational Information Seeking 

Conversational search is an IR task, in which a user’s information need is expressed 

through a natural language conversation with an IR system. The goal of an IR system is 

to elicit and formalize different aspects of the user’s information need through turns in a 

conversation. The key difference of conversational information seeking from other types of 

human-machine dialog is that information seeking dialogs are focused on identifying and

21 

obtaining target information from an information repository (e.g. a document collection 

or a knowledge graph). The key difference of conversational search from interactive IR 

[109, 11, 82, 156] is that interaction modality is a free-form natural language conversa-

tion. Conversational information seeking has been recently identified as one of the key 

emerging research directions in IR [37]. Several international workshops on conversa-

tional approaches to information retrieval [74, 135] and search-oriented conversational 

AI workshops [26, 31] have been held and established a foundation for future research in 

this area.

22 

CHAPTER 3 PARAMETERIZED FIELDED TERM DEPENDENCE MODELS FOR AD HOC ENTITY RETRIEVAL FROM KNOWLEDGE GRAPH 

Accurately matching unstructured keyword queries with structured entity representa-

tions for the task of ERKG is a fundamental theoretical problem, which didn’t receive a lot 

of research attention. 

In particular, existing retrieval models are based on a set of rigid assumptions, which 

limit their effectiveness for retrieval of structured entity documents. On one hand, re-

trieval models incorporating term dependencies, such as Sequential Dependence Model 

[96] (which allows to assign different importance weights to matching query concepts of 

different type), Weighted Sequential Dependence Model (WSDM) [13] (which estimates 

the importance of each matching query concept individually) and retrieval model based 

on copulas [48] disregard entity document structure by considering the matches of the 

same query concept in different fields of entity documents as equally important. On the 

other hand, although existing models for ad hoc structured document retrieval, such as the 

Mixture of Language Models (MLM) [110] and BM25F [122], factor in document struc-

ture when determining the degree of relevance of queries to documents, they do not take 

into account term dependencies (i.e. are agnostic to bigram query concepts). Further-

more, these models calculate the retrieval score of a structured document as a sum of the 

matching scores of each query term in a linear combination of the language models (LMs) 

for each document field. As a result, the field weights in this linear combination, which 

effectively determine the projection of query terms onto document fields, are the same for 

all query terms. Although the previously proposed Fielded Sequential Dependence Model 

(FSDM) [163] partially addressed this limitation by allowing different importance weights

23 

to the matches of a query concept in different fields of structured entity documents, such 

parametrization still lacks flexibility, as those weights are the same for all query concepts 

of the same type (unigrams, ordered and unordered bigrams). This can create a problem, 

which is illustrated by an example query “capitals in Europe which were host cities of sum-

mer Olympic games”. First, contrary to the assumption of FSDM, query concepts of the 

same type in this query should be projected onto different fields of relevant entity docu-

ments (e.g. “capitals” should be mapped onto the 

categories 

field, while “Europe” should be 

mapped onto the 

attributes 

field). Incorrect projection of any query concept (e.g. mapping 

“Europe” and “Olympic games” to the 

entity names 

field) is likely to substantially degrade 

the accuracy of retrieval results for this query. PRMS [79] learns a simple statistical rela-

tionship between the intended mapping of terms in free-text queries and their frequency in 

different document fields. Robust estimation of this relationship, however, requires query 

terms to have a non-uniform distribution across document fields and is negatively affected 

by data sparsity, particularly in the case of entity representations with a large number of 

fields. As a result, PRMS has inferior performance on entity retrieval tasks not only relative 

to FSDM [163], but also to both MLM and BM25F [9, 163]. 

To overcome the limitations of existing retrieval models, we propose the 

Parametrized 

Fielded Sequential Dependence Model 

(PFSDM) and the 

Parametrized Fielded Full De-

pendence 

Model 

(PFFDM), two novel feature-based retrieval models, which 

infer the user’s 

intent behind each individual query concept (unigram or bigram) by dynamically estimating 

its probabilistic mapping onto the fields of structured entity representations 

using a small 

number of statistical and linguistic features. We also provide a learning-to-rank algorithm 

to learn the weights of these features that maximize the target retrieval metric from the

24 

training data. The key contributions are as follows: 

1. We proposed PFSDM and PFFDM, two 

novel feature-based models for structured doc-

ument retrieval, 

which account for sequential and full term dependencies as well as 

provide flexible parametrization allowing to dynamically project each query concept 

onto document fields. To the best of our knowledge, there are no previous studies of 

feature-based models for structured document retrieval, in general, and ad hoc entity 

retrieval from knowledge graph, in particular; 

2. We propose a set of statistical and linguistic features of query concepts that enable their 

accurate projection onto the fields of structured entity documents; 

3. We experimentally demonstrate that, for the task of ad hoc entity retrieval from knowl-

edge graph, dynamic projection of query concepts onto entity representations is more 

effective than dynamic estimation of their importance. We also found out that retrieval 

models accounting for all dependencies between query terms provide more accurate 

retrieval results for this task than the models that account only for sequential depen-

dencies. 

3.1 Approach 

In this section, we introduce the ranking functions of Parameterized Fielded Sequential 

Dependence (PFSDM) and the Parameterized Fielded Full Dependence (PFFDM) retrieval 

models, the features used by these models to determine the projection of query concepts 

onto the fields of entity documents along with an algorithm to learn the weights of those 

features that maximize the target retrieval metric. 

The quality of retrieval results for entity-centric free-text queries depends on the cor-

rectness of inference of implicit query structure and the accuracy of matching the intent

25 

behind each query concept with different aspects of semantics of relevant entities encoded 

in their structured representations. However, the ambiguity of natural language can lead 

to many plausible interpretations of a keyword query, which combined with the require-

ment to accurately project those interpretations onto entity representations, makes entity 

retrieval from knowledge graph a challenging IR problem. 

PFSDM is a parametric extension of FSDM [163], a recently proposed MRF-based entity 

retrieval model, which takes into account 

both term dependencies and document structure. 

FSDM uses the following function to score each entity profile E with respect to a given 

keyword query Q:

In the case of entity descriptions with F fields, FSDM has 3 ∗ F + 3 parameters: F field 

mapping weights plus λT , λO and λU . We believe that this parametrization lacks the nec-

essary degrees of freedom, which can potentially limit the accuracy of this retrieval model.

wOqi,i+1,j = wUqi,i+1,j 

). PFSDM determines this projection based on multiple features, un-

like PRMS [79], which estimates it directly from the data based only on the total number 

of occurrences of a query term in a particular field across all documents in a collection. 

Feature-based estimation of this projection increases its robustness by overcoming the is-

sues of sparsity and uniform distribution of occurrences of a query concept across the fields 

of entity documents. 

PFFDM is different from PFSDM in that it accounts for all dependencies between the 

query terms, rather than only sequential ones. 

3.1.1 Features 

The features of different type that we propose to estimate the projection of a query 

concept κ onto field j of structured entity representations are presented in Table 1. In

28 

particular, PFSDM and PFFDM use two types of features: the ones whose value depends 

on a query concept and a field of entity representation and the ones that depend only on 

a query concept itself. The intuition behind also having the latter type of features is that 

the relation between them and the fields will be learned in the process of estimating their 

weights. For example, one can expect that the weight of a feature indicating whether a 

query concept is plural non-proper noun (NNS) will be higher in the 

categories 

field than 

in all other fields. For the features that depend on a field, one can expect that the value 

of the feature in that field will indicate the likelihood of a concept to be mapped to it. 

Nevertheless, we still learn the weights for these features, since: (1) ranges of values for 

particular features can be different in different fields and optimizing their weights is one 

of the ways to perform adequate scaling (2) contribution of the feature to the relevance of 

a field can be different for different fields. 

Two of the features (FP , TS) depend on the collection statistics of a particular field. 

During optimization and retrieval, these two real-valued features (FP , TS) were rescaled 

to [0, 1] range. The FP feature was rescaled logarithmically. 

The other group of field mapping features (NNP , NNS , JJS , NPP , NNO) are binary 

and take particular values based on the output of Standford POS Tagger or Parser. NNP 

takes positive values for the query concepts that are proper nouns (e.g. entity names) and, 

thus, should be mapped to the 

names, similar entity names 

and 

related entity names 

fields. 

The NNS , NPP , and NNO features take positive values for the concepts that designate 

a broader class or type of the desired entities and, therefore, should be mapped to the

3.1.2 Parameter Estimation 

In total, PFSDM and PFFDM have F ∗U +F ∗B + 3 parameters (F ∗U +F ∗B feature 

weights as well as λT , λO and λU), where F is the number of fields, while U and B are 

the number of field mapping features for unigrams and bigrams, respectively. An efficient 

two-stage block optimization algorithm for learning the parameters of PFSDM and PFFDM 

with respect to the target retrieval metric is presented in Algorithm 1. 

In the first stage (lines 3-6), the algorithm optimizes field mapping feature weights α 

separately for unigrams and bigrams. During optimization of the feature weights for uni-

grams, the feature weights for bigrams are not considered and vice versa. This is achieved 

by setting the corresponding λ weights to 0. After the algorithm is finished with optimizing 

the α weights, it proceeds to optimize the weights of MRF potential functions for different 

query concept types (λT , λO and λU in Eq. 3.1).

3.2 Experiments 

3.2.1 Experimental Setup 

Experimental results reported were obtained on a publicly available benchmark devel-

oped by Balog and Neumayer [9], which uses DBpedia as the knowledge graph. For fair 

comparison, we used the same five field entity representation scheme and the same query 

sets as in [163] (SemSearch ES consisting primarily of named entity queries, ListSearch 

consisting primarily of entity list search queries, QALD-2 consisting of entity-focused natu-

ral language questions, and INEX-LD containing a mix of entity-centric queries of different 

type). We pre-processed both entity documents and queries by applying the Krovetz stem-

mer and removing the stopwords in the INQUERY stopword list. 

3.2.2 Feature Analysis 

First, to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed features, we performed an ex-

ploratory analysis of distributions of their values (for the features whose values depend 

on document fields) or frequencies of their occurrences (for the features whose values are 

independent of document fields) in different fields of entity representations. Specifically, 

we manually annotated each concept in all queries according to the user’s intent with re-

spect to a particular aspect of target entities as an 

attribute 

concept, 

entity 

concept,

concept. Our intuition is that the

query concepts (e.g. when a

occurring or have relatively higher feature values in the 

attributes 

field of entity represen-

tations. Query terms or phrases marked as 

entity 

concepts (e.g. when a user is searching 

for a particular named entity) should be primarily occurring in the 

names

similar en-

tity names

trieval models and the baselines have been optimized using 5-fold cross validation (except
